findings.evidence_excerpt:
Greek seas, has yet to see comparable systematic archaeological engagement, despite evidence of sustained
pirate and privateer activity throughout the early modern period (e.g., Krantonelli 1985, 1991, 1998; Harlaftis
et al. 2016). Recent studies by George Koutzakiotis (2023, this volume) demonstrate the potential of integrating
­archaeological research with the rich documentary evidence of the period, revealing promising avenues for the
 study of piracy in this region.
    A similar paucity of archaeological studies is evident for piracy in classical antiquity. A pioneering example
linking specific archaeological finds to the phenomenon of piracy was advanced by Antonios Keramopoullos
(1923, 42–3), who argued that the seventeen shackled individuals uncovered during Konstantinos Kourouniotis
and Stratis Pelekidis’ excavations at Phaleron were probably pirates executed for their deeds (see also Bosnakis
2020, 159–69). Otherwise, references to piracy in the archaeological literature have been few and, when they do
appear, they are typically brief and interpreted from a victims’ perspective. Some have pointed to the numerous
Late Classical and Hellenistic towers situated on islands and along the eastern Mediterranean mainland coast,
to suggest that these functioned as bastions to protect coastal communities and private landowners from pirate
raids (e.g., Ormerod 1924a, 41–3; 1924b, 31–2; Young 1956, 132–33; Osborne 1986, 173–74; Pritchett 1991,
352–58; Seifried and Parkinson 2014, 310). Likewise, the intense piracy that plagued the Aegean in the first half
of the 1st century BCE has led many scholars to attribute the contemporaneous evidence of violent d     ­ estruction
at Delos to pirate raids that are reported to have occurred there in 88 and 69 BCE (e.g., Mattingly 1980; Rauh
1993, 68; Hatzidakis 1997, 293, 307; Siebert 2001, 93; Rotroff 2014). Vassilis Lambrinoudakis (1981, 161; 1987–
1988, 299) has suggested that a destruction layer dated to the early 1st century BCE at the sanctuary of Apollo
Maleatas in Epidaurus is likewise attributable to a pirate assault.
    In addition to studies that rely on archaeological data to address the likely impact of piracy on the wider
public, some researchers have attempted to utilize archaeological remains to identify the likely habitats and
operational bases of pirates themselves. Probably the most systematic archaeological research of ancient ­piracy
to date is the Rough Cilicia Archaeological Survey Project, directed by Nicholas Rauh (1997, 2003, 2004, 2019;
see also Rauh et al. 2000, 2009, 2013, Kaye and Rauh 2020, Hoff et al. 2024, as well as Dawson and Rauh, this
volume), which, from 1996 to 2014, attempted to identify the settlements and hideouts of the notorious ­Cilician
pirates along the coast of modern day Gazipasha, Turkey (for the Cilician pirates see also Avidov 2008; Zoroğlu
2009; Tomaschitz 2013). Beginning in the mid-1980s, Elpida Hadjidaki (2001, 2015, 2020) has been directing the
systematic excavation of ancient Phalasarna, a polis in western Crete closely associated with ­Hellenistic piracy.
Since 2000, Aris Tsaravopoulos (2015, 2023; see also Johnston et al. 2012; Kozatsas et al. 2014; T­ saravopoulos
and Kroustalis, this volume) has been excavating the site of Antikythera, a colony of Phalasarna, that is likewise
presumed to have functioned as a pirate base. Meanwhile, Adonis Kyrou (1990, 137–41; 1996–1997; see also
Lolos 2006) has persuasively argued that the fortified hill of Choriza on the island of Hydra served as a base
for Samian pirates, who were active around 530 BCE. Yet another category of remains plausibly linked to pi-
racy, those of ancient shipsheds, straddles the boundary between terrestrial and underwater archaeology (Baika
2007–2008; Blackman et al. 2013, 238–41; see also Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis, this volume on the shipshed
at Antikythera).
     This last-mentioned category (shipsheds) shifts attention to the main stage of pirate operations, namely the
sea, and to the material evidence recovered by underwater archaeology. The methodological challenges con-
fronting underwater archaeologists who attempt to associate underwater remains with piracy notwithstanding
(see Gianfrotta 1981, 2001, 2013, and Koutsouflakis, this volume), several finds recovered through marine
­archaeology have gained credence in the discussion. These include a helmet containing part of a human skull
 that was recovered from the early 1st-century BCE at Spargi in the Madalena Archipelago (Gianfrotta 1981,
 2001, 2013; Cavazzuti 1997, 2004; Bruni 2013).
    Perhaps the most significant underwater discovery to date to conjure the prospect of piracy is undoubtedly
the wreck of the ancient merchant ship found near Kyrenia, in northern Cyprus. The Kyrenia shipwreck is dated
quite precisely due to its closed context of cargoes to 294–290 BCΕ. Scholars have raised compelling arguments

the preference for more conventional explanations –for
 instance, ­imported objects are typically interpreted as evidence of trade or elite gift exchange– or to an im-
 plicit a­ ssumption that piracy, as a historically elusive and mobile practice, leaves no imperceptible trace in the
 ­archaeological record.
    The methodological difficulty of identifying the archaeological remains of piracy has been emphasized by
numerous scholars (e.g., Cavazzuti 2004, 51; Baika 2007–2008, 56, 61, 68; Bruni 2013, 766; Gianfrotta 2013, 53;
Hartnett and Dawdy 2013, 40; Rauh 2019, 49). The problem stems primarily from the fact that the material re-
mains of pirates are often indistinguishable from those of wider, “law-abiding”, society. For example, structures
and ships employed by pirates frequently resembled those employed by the general public, in the same manner
that the destruction inflicted on an ancient settlement by a pirate raid might resemble that of a military assault.
What seems crucial is that archaeologists assess the question within an interpretive framework, one that con-
siders piracy as a fluid, dynamic phenomenon with the potential to shape local and regional economies and, at
times, to catalyze political and social transformations in any given era. This interpretive framework is precisely
what the A.P.Pir.A. project has intended to create.

Scope and objectives
Hosted by the Department of History and Archaeology at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, the
A.P.Pir.A. project transpired between January 2021 and June 2024, with funding from the H  ­ ellenic F
                                                                                                     ­ oundation
for Research and Innovation. The research team consisted of seven archaeologists, led by the present author
as principal investigator, alongside Nadia Giagkoudaki, Orestis Goulakos, Panagiotis Gounelas, Alexandra
­Malliou, Konstantinos Pantzouris and Dimitris N. Sakkas. Throughout the duration of the project, this small
 group of early-career researchers attempted to construct a spatially diachronic approach to the archaeology of
 piracy. Our aim was to develop a framework through which piracy could be meaningfully integrated into the
 archaeological discourse, a framework sufficiently broad to incorporate evidence of piracy across the breadth
 of the eastern Mediterranean Sea and across a timeframe extending from the Final Neolithic to the Roman era
 (ca. 4000 BCE – 330 CE).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Methodology and research implementation
The project unfolded in four distinct stages. The initial phase focused on piracy in classical antiquity, specifically
from the Archaic to the Roman period. This decision has the obvious advantage of drawing on the information
provided by literary sources about piracy to allow for more comprehensive analysis. Textual references pro-
vide the added value of furnishing detailed information about piracy that can be cross-referenced against the
­extensive archaeological record of the same era.
    To facilitate systematic documentation and analysis, the team developed a digital database using the open-
source online platform Heurist. Design by the author of this paper, the database is intended to record, manage
and analyze material drawn from a wide range of ancient Greek and Latin sources (e.g., historical narratives,
oratory and inscriptions) that contain either explicit or implicit allusions to pirate activity in the Greek maritime
world during the period in question. The entries –compiled primarily by A.P.Pir.A. research team members
Orestis Goulakos and Konstantinos Pantzouris– amount to nearly 500 records and have yielded tremendous
insights into the historical evolution of piracy in classical antiquity, the operational strategies of pirates and
the manner in which they were perceived by their contemporaries. This database constitutes a comprehensive
repository that will facilitate the systematic study of ancient piracy through textual evidence.
     For example, the analysis of the statistical data derived from the database reveals that, while piracy ­appears
to have been a continually recurring phenomenon throughout classical antiquity, the Hellenistic period (323–27
BCE) stands out as a peak moment of pirate activity, particularly in the eastern Mediterranean basin. These
­findings validate two fundamental conclusions: first, that piracy constituted an endemic feature of the maritime
 landscape of classical antiquity; and second, that sustained efforts to suppress piracy by naval powers, such as
 Athens, Rhodes and Rome, achieved limited and temporary success at best (on this issue see de Souza 1999,
 38–41, 48–53, 83–4, 161–78, 184, 204–10; Lampinen 2022, 52–3; also, on Rhodes and Rome’s campaigns against
 piracy, see respectively Kalmpourtzi, and Dawson and Rauh, this volume).
     Following the study of the written sources, a systematic correlation was undertaken between the
a­ rchaeological evidence and the data extracted from the database. This process facilitated the formulation of
 specific archaeological criteria and attributes derived from the material record that may under certain condi-
 tions be applicable to the phenomenon of piracy. For example, a list of representative features emerged that
 appear to characterize an archaeologically identifiable pirate base, that is, a settlement where a portion of the
 population, however large or small, engaged occasionally or habitually in piracy. The scale of such bases ranges
 widely from small encampments to full-fledged cities. Importantly, the material remains of these sites often
 do not diverge significantly from those of conventional settlements, thereby making their identification all the

more challenging. Nevertheless, pirate bases do tend to display fundamental recurring traits that assist with
their recognition. These can be grouped into four broad thematic categories:
    1. Chronological context
    •    Evidence that a given site was occupied during a period when piracy is known to have been prevalent
         in the vicinity. Establishing the habitational time frame of a settlement within the context of known
         piratical disturbances seems prerequisite to drawing a connection between the two.
    2. Spatial and geomorphological characteristics
    •    Site selection: Pirate bases are frequently situated in coastal areas that offer concealment or limited
         visibility from the sea and/or mainland. These sites exploit natural topographical advantages, yet are
         strategically positioned in proximity to important maritime routes.
    •    Suitability for pirate operations: Pirate suitability is typically linked to topographical features, such
         as bays, coves or natural harbors, that facilitate ambushes, provide shelter and enable eavesdropping
         on passing sea traffic. In certain instances, the suitability of a location is further corroborated by the
         chronological reuse of the exact same site or an adjacent location as pirate bases, most likely because
         the physical and strategic advantages of the site lent themselves to recurring use by pirates over time.
    •    Anomalous sites and finds: Some sites are situated in locations that appear, at first glance, wholly
         ­unsuitable for permanent habitation or harbor development (e.g., barren terrain, lack of accessible an-
          chorages). When settings such as these reveal the presence of “unanticipated” valuable, high-status
          ­artifacts, the likelihood that they served an atypical or illicit function becomes archaeologically relevant.
    3. Functional and structural features
    •    Short-lived occupation: Particularly in the case of small settlements, the archaeological record may point
         to a temporally limited or episodic occupation, often interpreted as opportunistic or purpose-built,
         rather than part of a long-term habitation pattern.
    •    Fortification systems: In addition to natural defenses, some sites exhibit evidence of artificial
         ­reinforcement through constructed for

         ­connection between the inhabitants’ economic or subsistence strategies and the sea. This may be
          ­reflected in the presence of maritime artifacts, infrastructure or iconographic motifs.
    •    Martial character: The presence of weaponry, martial iconography or other artifacts associated with the
         use of violence may point to a community familiar with or habituated to armed conflict. While such
         indicators are not exclusive to piracy, their co-occurrence with other characteristics described above
         strengthens the argument for pirate occupation.
    It should be emphasized that the presence of one or even several of these traits does not by itself confirm the
identification of a given site as a pirate base. Nor is the combination of all these features required to justify such
an interpretation. Obviously, the greater the number and consistency of such indicators at a given site, the more
compelling the need to include pirate activity within a range of archaeological interpretations. For instance,
the application of the above criteria, in conjunction with the analysis of literary sources on ancient piracy, led
Konstantinos Pantzouris to propose that the fortified site at Kastraki on Agathonisi may not have served solely
as a defensive outpost safeguarding Miletus and its maritime trade against the pirates, who were particularly
active in the region during the Hellenistic period. Rather, the site itself may have participated in pirate activity
–likely targeting non-Milesian interests– thereby functioning both as a protective and a predatory node within
the complex maritime landscape of the time (see Pantzouris, this volume).
    The establishment of archaeological criteria for the identification of piracy enabled the team to proceed to
the second phase of the project, namely the investigation of piracy during periods, when archaeological data

 Nonetheless, as both Nadia Giagkoudaki’s study on the origins of piracy in the EBA Aegean and Panagiotis

Dissemination and public engagement
As part of the A.P.Pir.A. project, the Museum of Cycladic Art (MCA) participated as a collaborating institution,
for the purpose of undertaking both the design and the production of an educational program featuring piracy
in antiquity. Upon completion of the research phase, the A.P.Pir.A. research team submitted a detailed report to
the MCA’s Department of Educational and Social Programs. This report marked the beginning of the project’s
third phase, which was intended to develop the educational component. The report included extensive data
on ancient piracy, descriptions of relevant archaeological sites and finds, as well as suggestions for the educa-
tional program’s structure and activities. Drawing on this material, the MCA’s team of dedicated museologists
proceeded to generate the educational program, entitled “Piracy in the Cyclades”. Directed toward an audience
of students age eight and above, the program comprises teaching resources, suggested activities and an educa-
tional board game. As Eleni Markou elaborates in her contribution to this volume, the program was designed
for flexible use both within the MCA and in school settings, ensuring nation-wide accessibility for teachers and
students alike.
      The final phase of the A.P.Pir.A. project focused on the dissemination of its research outcomes. The
­international hybrid conference “The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity”, held under the auspices of the
 ­Department of History and Archaeology of the NKUA on October 5–6, 2023, along with the publication of its
  proceedings in the present volume, represent key elements of this effort. The decision to organize an interna-
  tional hybrid conference stemmed from the research team’s intent not only to present the results of our work,
  but also to engage with scholars working on related aspects of ancient piracy in order to generate a productive
  academic dialog.
    Beyond the international conference, the A.P.Pir.A. team undertook a variety of additional activities ­intended
to promote communication and dissemination. Among them was the participation of Panagiotis Gounelas and
the present author in the international hybrid conference “Nostoi II: Traveling in the Eastern Mediterranean Sea
and Inland Routes from the Early Bronze Age to the End of the Early Iron Ages”, held at the Acropolis Museum
from 11 to 13 November 2022. The conference proceedings, soon to be published under the editorship of Kon-
stantinos Kopanias, Çiğdem Maner, Nikolaos Stampolidis and Ioannis Fappas, will include our paper entitled
“‘Who Are You, Strangers?’ The Contribution of the Homeric Epics to the Study of Ancient Piracy”. This study
explores the phenomenon of piracy as it appears in the Homeric epics and examines the usefulness of these
literary sources to the investigation of piracy in antiquity (Samaras and Gounelas forthcoming).
   Additionally, the present author has prepared a study entitled “Fortifications in the Middle and Late Bronze
Age Aegean: When, Where and Why?”, which is forthcoming in the edited volume Polemika: Perceptions of
Warfare in the Bronze Age Aegean, to be published under the direction of Kyriakos Grigoropoulos, Angelos

tems of central and southern mainland and insular Greece during the MBA and LBA. Its primary ­objective is to
assess the various factors that prompted their construction. The analysis suggests that, with minimal ­exception,
the Aegean region experienced persistent insecurity throughout the second millennium BCE. This insecurity
appears to have been driven sometimes by local competition and at other times by the endemic ­phenomenon

­settlements.
    Throughout the duration of the A.P.Pir.A. project, the team paid particular attention to outreach ­initiatives
intended to engage the broader public. Chief among these was the aforementioned educational program de-
veloped by the MCA. In addition, the project maintained a consistent presence on social media through its
Facebook page (APPirA – Archaeological Research Project) and Instagram account (@appira_project), both
of which were managed by Alexandra Malliou. These platforms were used to showcase dissemination activities
and selected research findings, as well as to present various aspects of ancient piracy in a clear and accessible
manner. The public response was remarkably positive, indicating substantial interest in the topic and high-
lighting the degree to which the archaeology of piracy resonates with wider audiences. Finally, a dedicated

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Research outcomes and archaeological challenges
As a concise evaluation of the research results of the A.P.Pir.A. project, the findings can be described as highly
encouraging. The project successfully identified specific sites that either conceivably served as pirate bases or
were assaulted by pirate raids and it recognized potential components of pirate activity across various catego-
ries of artifacts (e.g., pottery, rock-engravings, seals). Furthermore, the research demonstrated that during the
extensive time frame under consideration, the levels of pirate activity in the Greek seas varied significantly,
ranging from isolated incidents of piracy to sustained periods of piracy capable of influencing the outcome of
political events. Periods of heightened pirate activity, identified with varying degrees of certainty, include the
EBA II (ca. 2700–2200 BCE), the Postpalatial period (ca. 1200–1050 BCE), the Geometric period (ca. 900–700
BCE), the Archaic period (ca. 700–480 BCE) and the Hellenistic period (ca. 323–67 BCE). Notably, these phases
often coincide with episodes of political disintegration, economic disturbance or weakened public authority –
highlighting the interplay between piracy and wider societal transformations.
       Perhaps even more significantly, the project contributed to a deeper understanding of the fundamental
­challenges that confront the archaeology of piracy. As mentioned above, pirates rarely left behind material
 ­evidence of their activities, and when they did, such traces were often indistinguishable from those of con-
  temporary “law-abiding” communities. The A.P.Pir.A. project underscores the limitations of traditional
  ­archaeological paradigms, which have too often underestimated the archaeological signature of piracy or dis-
   missed it as ­archaeologically “invisible” or marginal. In addition, the project revealed two key findings that
   suggest that an archaeological approach to piracy is indeed feasible, despite the methodological challenges: (1)
   Despite regional and chronological variations, piracy exhibited distinct diachronic features, not only in terms
   of operational practices and areas of activity but also in terms of the perceptions of piracy that prevailed in
   public consciousness; (2) Pirate activity does leave a strong archaeological signature, which is detectable when
   subjected to innovative, interdisciplinary and critically reflexive methodologies. Only through such approaches
   can the archaeology of piracy move beyond the perception of an elusive or marginal phenomenon and establish
   itself as a productive field of inquiry, capable of offering new insights into the dynamics of maritime violence
   and its impact on ancient societies.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Identifying ancient pirate bases
The results of the A.P.Pir.A. project, together with the studies presented in this volume, underline both the
­challenges and the prospects of developing an archaeology of piracy. Despite methodological and interpretive
 difficulties, archaeological research has proven capable of identifying sites that may have functioned as pirate
 bases across different regions and periods. Well-known examples include Choriza on Hydra, ­Phalasarna in
 western Crete and Antikythera (see above; also Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis, this volume). Furthermore, some
 of the contributions to this volume point to potential pirate involvement at other sites of classical ­antiquity
 (particularly during the Hellenistic period), such as Kastraki on Agathonisi (Pantzouris) and the islet of
 ­Antidragonera, close to Kythera (Markakis).
    Crucially, the field is no longer confined to historical periods with textual evidence but now extends to
prehistoric and proto-historical contexts. Sites such as Strophilas on Andros and Vathy on Astypalaia indicate
possible pirate activity already in the Late Neolithic and Early Helladic I periods (Giagkoudaki). The likeli-
hood appears even greater at certain Early Cycladic settlements (Angelopoulou; Giagkoudaki), with the site
of Kastri on Syros standing out alongside those of Panormos on Naxos, Kynthos on Delos and Markiani on
Amorgos. In the LBA, and particularly in its final stages, several sites in Cyprus (e.g., Pyla-Kokkinokremos,
Maa-­Palaiokastro) and Crete (e.g., Pseira, Mochlos, Kastri at Palaikastro, Elias to Nisi, Kalo Chorafi, Korakia
on Dia, Kastrokephala) likely served, at least in part, as pirate bases (Driessen; Vokotopoulos). Comparable
patterns persist through the transition to the EIA and across the period itself, as evidenced by Meganisi in the
Inner Ionian Archipelago (Vikatou and Staikou) and by a series of coastal and island sites in the Aegean that are
discussed by Panagiotis Gounelas.
    The systematic reconsideration of such sites as potential pirate bases will contribute to the identification
of the structural and spatial characteristics of early pirate settlements and to the elucidation of their material
culture. This perspective is particularly valuable at locations where pirate activity appears to have been more
than episodic, constituting instead a communal way of life, as has been suggested with the examples of Pyla-­
Kokkinokremos in Cyprus and Meganisi in the Inner Ionian Archipelago (Driessen; Vikatou and Staikou).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Topography and persistent pirate activity
Several studies in this volume emphasize the importance of coastal topography to the location of recurring
pirate disorders. Contributions by Adam Dawson and Nicholas Rauh on Cilicia, George Koutsouflakis on the
Phournoi archipelago, Nirefs Markakis on Kythera, and Olympia Vikatou and Vivian Staikou on the C      ­ entral Io-
nian Sea collectively demonstrate that regions with nonlinear coastlines, that is, those characterized by ­islands,
inlets and coves offering concealment, narrow sea passages that forced merchant vessels to travel at reduced
speed and alongside predictable sailing routes, as well as heavily trafficked maritime corridors rich in commer-
cial targets, experienced recurring patterns of piracy. Within this framework, the area associated with the noto-
rious Liburnian pirates, discussed by Filip Budić, though far less studied than Cilicia, the Aegean or the Ionian,
emerges as a particularly promising field of research, combining topographical suitability with a well-attested
pirate tradition.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Fortifications and defensive strategies
Another critical yet ambivalent component in the archaeology of piracy highlighted in several ­contributions
to this volume is the presence of fortifications. While, as Jan Driessen emphasizes, pirates occasionally
erected their own defenses, they more typically appropriated existing structures. The tendency to associate
well-­constructed fortifications with organized polities does not preclude their use by pirates, as the sites of
­Phalasarna, ­Antikythera and those in Cilicia demonstrate (Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis; Dawson and Rauh).

Rather, the remains of fortified sites (especially smaller bastions nestled along remote coastlines) underline
the multiplicity of functions that defenses could assume, functioning sometimes as bulwarks against piracy
and at other times as strongholds for pirate bands themselves, as argued by Konstantinos Pantzouris for the
fortified site of Kastraki on A
                              ­ gathonisi. In fact, through his recent archival and field research about the occu-
pation of particular A­ egean islands by pirates and corsairs of the 17th century, George Koutzakiotis (2023, this
volume) corroborates Driessen’s view that pirates themselves typically resorted to makeshift, hastily constructed
structures (see also Dawson and Rauh, this volume on the survival of Hellenistic fortifications employing a
­“vernacular” masonry technique in coastal Rough Cilicia and their potential link to piracy).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Beyond stereotypes: wealth, prosperity and pirate settlements
It is equally essential to challenge entrenched stereotypes that restrict our understanding of piracy and restrain
its archaeological study, such as the assumption that pirate settlements were invariably small, impoverished and
littoral. As Jan Driessen observes, “the size and prosperity of a coastal settlement do not exclude its role as a po-
tential pirate’s nest”. Indeed, the presence of exotica and wealth, normally interpreted as evidence of prosperity
resulting from commercial exchanges, may, in fact, reflect pirate occupation. This seems particularly plausible at
modest coastal settlements, such as Mochlos and Petras in eastern Crete. The presence of luxury goods at these
sites suggest that they functioned as pirate hideouts or as safe havens, where pirates could obtain provisions and
exchange plunder for foodstuffs.
    Adam Dawson and Nicholas Rauh’s study of the Cilician pirates further clarifies potential modes of o  ­ peration
through the selection of “occluded sites” by ancient pirate bands. These scholars demonstrate how pirates situ-
ated in coastal centers along vulnerable sea-lanes maintained visual contact with seaborne targets indirectly by
communicating with lookouts situated at occluded satellite sites in the highland interior. Strategically positioned
to observe maritime traffic while remaining invisible from the sea, the inland lookouts potentially delivered
early-warning signals to pirate bands waiting along the coast. This pattern, substantiated through systematic
surface survey and GIS analysis, is valuable not only for reconstructing evidence of ancient pirate practices, but
also for demonstrating the need to incorporate the investigation of interior sites into the archaeology of piracy.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Funerary contexts and mortuary display
A similar interpretative approach applies to funerary contexts. Jan Driessen suggests that the presence of exotica
and valuable artifacts, especially when combined with weaponry, in burials such as the Griffin Warrior’s tomb
at Pylos or the rich grave excavated by Nikolaos Platon on Skopelos might be attributable to successful pirate
raids. Panagiotis Gounelas has similarly argued that certain EIA burials, such as Tomb 79 at Lefkandi, may
represent instances where wealth, possibly acquired in part through piracy, was manifested through mortuary
display. More broadly, in periods of demonstrable or particularly intense levels of pirate activity and in regions
topographically suited to such practices, the combination of exotica, prestige goods and weaponry in burial
assemblages should at least raise the possibility that the interred person had engaged in piracy.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Piracy in visual arts
Piracy’s cultural impact also resonates in the visual arts, despite the tendency of ancient artistic production to
focus on elites and to underrepresent the everyday activities of social inferiors. The unnerving impact of pirate
activity on the public consciousness all but insured its occasional depiction. Several well-known works ranging
from the Flotilla Fresco at Akrotiri, the Siege Rhyton from Mycenae (Driessen; Sakas) and the depiction of
Ramses III’s naval battle against the Sea Peoples in the Medinet Habu relief in Egypt (Ladas) to the Middle
Geometric krater 31.11.2 in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (Gounelas) and the Late Archaic cup B436 in the
British Museum (Manakidou), have all been interpreted as representations of piracy.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Some contributions to this volume suggest that these depictions are potentially more numerous than
­ reviously recognized; however, their import has been subsumed under more standard interpretations. For
p
instance, the rock engraving at Korphi t’Aroniou, that depicts an armed man leading an animal in a boat,
more convincingly illustrates animal theft –a timeless pirate practice– than it does livestock transportation
­(Giagkoudaki). Likewise, Eleni Manakidou has drawn attention to a small group of late red-figure vases and
 late Panathenaic amphorae depicting Athena or Nike holding the aphlaston, namely, the decorated stern of an
ancient ship. While most representations of this motif date to the second quarter of the 5th century BCE and
are conventionally associated with events during the Persian Wars, most particularly, the naval battle at Salamis,
this later group may instead allude to other forms of Athenian maritime success, including naval victories over
pirates.
     In any event, it should be emphasized that visual sources, much like textual ones, tend to frame piracy
through narratives of success. Regardless of whether the artwork depicts victories over pirates or successful
­pirate raids, specific historical events or broader reflections of maritime supremacy, such representations are
 consistently articulated from the victor’s perspective. Even mythological scenes –most notably the popular
 story of Dionysus’ attempted abduction by Tyrrhenian pirates, examined in detail by Stamatis Fritzilas in this
 volume– reflect contemporary familiarity with piracy and similar historical realities potentially embedded in
 myths.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
The maritime sphere and underwater archaeology
  Turning to the pirates’ main sphere of activity –the sea– it seems that, for the moment, its contribution to
  the ­archaeology of piracy remains limited. Scholars broadly agree that in both prehistoric times and ­classical
­antiquity ships employed for piracy –whether systematic or opportunistic– did not differ substantially from
 contemporary vessels (see Giagkoudaki on the EBA; Tsonakas on the LBA; Nakas on the Classical and
 ­Hellenistic periods). A constant requirement of pirate ships in all eras was speed, maneuverability and stealth-
  iness; ­nevertheless, it must always be borne in mind that even the humblest craft could be employed for pirate
  purposes.
    Underwater archaeology faces long-recognized difficulties in linking finds directly to piracy (see above), a
point also emphasized by George Koutsouflakis in his study of the Phournoi archipelago in the eastern Aegean.
Nevertheless, the Kyrenia shipwreck and recent studies on it provide reasons for optimism that careful excava-
tion and systematic study of shipwrecks will illuminate future pirate contexts, as has already been shown with
early modern examples (e.g., de Bry 2006; Lizé 2006; de Bry and Roling 2016; Soulat et al. 2023; see also Page
and Ewen 2016). To this evidence may now be added shipwreck no. 23 that sank off the modern settlement
of Bali in Phournoi. The wreck is dated to the early 19th century and was apparently scuttled after capture
and plunder (Koutsouflakis). Furthermore, as the same scholar rightly concludes, combining terrestrial and
­underwater data holds the potential to reconstruct patterns of pirate activity in regions of particular interest.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Future directions and concluding remarks
The archaeology of piracy in antiquity is progressing with increasing methodical rigor and organization,
­providing fresh avenues for future research. This view is fully confirmed by George Koutzakiotis’ contribution,
 which effectively “closes the curtain” on this volume by examining piracy and the corso in the Aegean during
 early modern times, a period more accessible archaeologically than is antiquity. Two main categories of mate-
 rial culture relevant to piracy have been identified: (1) remains directly linked to pirate activity and the need
 to secure ships, loot and personnel; and (2) everyday objects and artifacts. For the first category, geographical
 context is decisive: such finds occur in locations otherwise inexplicable or uniquely suitable for piracy. For the
 second, although direct association is difficult to prove, Koutzakiotis reminds us that pirates were embedded in
 the societies of their time, sharing the same essential needs as their contemporaries.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
In general, considering the factors outlined above (such as the importance of topography and the p    ­ ositive
correlation between piracy and maritime trade), promising contexts for investigating ancient piracy include
­regions that display a combination of favorable geomorphology, a pirate tradition and periods of robust mari-
 time trade. The fact that such examples are numerous in Greek seas and across the wider Mediterranean does
 not diminish the phenomenon, but rather highlights its potential scope and dispersal. When such conditions
 ­correspond with additional indicators, like coastal fortifications, “hidden” or “inconvenient” settlements,
  weapons in ships or burials, or martial imagery displayed in maritime settings, piracy should at least be in-
  cluded among the interpretative possibilities. Furthermore, case studies such as those of Adam Dawson and
  Nicholas Rauh on Cilicia and Nirefs Markakis on Kythera demonstrate the potential of GIS analyses to the study
  of ancient piracy. Finally, Jan Driessen’s advice to “focus on time periods during which major state organizations
  were either absent or weakened” seems particularly useful and is confirmed in nearly every contribution to this
  volume. As Leonidas Vokotopoulos points out, in times of political and social instability there were always those
  who perceived turbulence not as a problem but as an opportunity.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Until recently, archaeologists have largely avoided addressing piracy, owing to the methodological and
­interpretive difficulties involved. Pirates themselves often sought to conceal their activities, while the mate-
 rial culture associated with piracy rarely differed in any substantial way from that of other activities, such as
 trade or warfare. Nevertheless, piracy was an endemic feature of the ancient Mediterranean world, embedded
 in everyday life across multiple periods, and at times capable of influencing political, economic and social
 ­developments. For this reason, it is incumbent upon archaeological researchers to develop methodologies ca-
  pable of overcoming these challenges and addressing the phenomenon of piracy, thereby sharing a burden that
  has ­hitherto been borne almost exclusively by text-dependent historians. Beyond the chronological limitations
  inherent to historical research, several studies in this volume –such as Adam Dawson and Nicholas Rauh’s
  examination of Cilician piracy in the late Hellenistic period and George Koutsouflakis’s work on the Phournoi
  archipelago in the early modern era– underscore the literary hyperbole about piracy that is frequently encoun-
  tered in written sources and the consequent need for careful deconstruction. Archaeologists must, therefore,
  proceed in lock step with historians by addressing dimensions that are otherwise inaccessible to textual analysis,
  but are capable at the same time of providing an essential means of cross-reference written testimony, regardless
  of whether that testimony magnifies the scope and intensity of piracy and downplays and obscures it.
     The contributions to this volume highlight both the difficulties and the possibilities for the pursuit of the
archaeology of piracy and demonstrate that pirates left ambiguous but recognizable traces. Settlements, for-
tifications, destruction horizons, iconography and funerary assemblages may all reflect pirate activity when
subjected to appropriate contextual analysis. Case studies such as those of Aris Tsaravopoulos and Evangelos
­Kroustalis on the Antikythera shipwreck or Nirefs Markakis on Antidragonera suggest that certain sites and
 finds may in fact be best understood through the lens of piracy. The most promising directions for future re-
 search include closer integration of archaeological and textual evidence, GIS analyses, sustained attention to
 the role of slaving and ransom markets in shaping maritime economies, and greater focus on the experiences of
 victims and non-elite actors, who are all too often eclipsed in state-centered narratives.
    Above all, we must remember that seafaring identities were fluid: merchants might become pirates and
pirates could be turned into merchants or serve as naval auxiliaries. Such multiplicity, highlighted in several
contributions to this volume, underscores the complex social realities of maritime life in antiquity and suggests
that the archaeology of piracy should avoid one-dimensional approaches. Piracy should not be viewed merely
as an instrument of disruption. As Carla Antonaccio has noted (2017, 223), it could also serve as a force of

findings.evidence_excerpt:
c­ onnectivity and mobility. Viewed in this light, piracy emerges not simply as criminal predation at sea but as
 a dynamic phenomenon situated at the intersection of commerce, warfare and diplomacy, embedded within
 networks of marginality, informal exchange and both resistance to and collaboration with established powers.
   We may never uncover an archaeological find that can be indisputably associated with ancient piracy. No
archaeologist realistically anticipates discovering a ship bearing a pirate flag, a buried treasure chest or a grave
with a stele explicitly identifying its occupant as a pirate. The A.P.Pir.A. project sought to transcend the treat-
ment of piracy as a marginal topic or footnote and to re-situate it within archaeological discourse as a dynamic
and multifaceted phenomenon deeply embedded in ancient societies. The contributions assembled in this
volume advance precisely this goal: they establish piracy as a legitimate subject of archaeological investigations
and invite us to begin reflecting on and engaging with the figure of the ancient pirates. In other words, the
journey into the archaeology of piracy in antiquity is still in its infancy…

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The almost honorable regard for sea raiders in Homer contrasts considerably with Thucydides’ well-known ­assertion
that Minos freed the seas from piracy, suggesting a major switch in appreciation in the ways foreign goods and slaves
were acquired in the Iron Age and how piracy affected state formation. Is Homer’s attitude closer to that of the ­situation
in the Bronze Age? Or of one phase of the Bronze Age when raiding was a general custom and a way of life? Apart from
synthesizing work by other scholars on pirates and piracy at various moments during the Aegean Bronze Age, I review
the nature and location of settlements, representations of naval warfare and raiding, as well as the p­ resence of exotica
potentially resulting from what Renfrew called “negative reciprocity” for what these can inform us on the existence of
“sea thieves”. I also discuss the sites of Pyla-Kokkinokremos and Maa-Palaiokastro on Cyprus and their potential link to
piracy or the Sea Peoples in general.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The romanticized picture of piracy presented in movies and literature, as we all know, does not agree with reality
– pirates were the scourge of the seas and still are, even if the number of pirate attacks is going down (Shane and
Magnuson 2016). While most of the Mediterranean is relatively safe nowadays, the Libyan coast has seen an
increase of pirate attacks, with ships venturing further away from the coast and threatening passing merchant
ships (Robitaille 2020). Other attacks have been noted in the Gulf of Guinea and the Straits of Singapore but, in
contrast, Somali piracy is now negligeable due to international policing in the Arabian Gulf (Soğancilar 2021;
Sandkamp et al. 2022).
     The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity, the topic of this volume, was already a theme of interest to scholars
during WW I (Semple 1916), but I will, for obvious reasons, focus on Bronze Age Crete. There is evidently a
problem of anachronistically attributing later connotations, since the island had a bad reputation not only in
Hellenistic and early Roman times and in the 9th and 10th centuries CE, when Arabs originally from Spain used
it as their base for pirate attacks in the Aegean (Christides 1984), but also later when, despite Venetian and later
Ottoman control, it was on the receiving end, being plagued by Barbary pirates (Davis 2017; Dimitropoulos
2022).
    Finding material traces of piracy is not an easy task neither for historical, nor for prehistoric times, since
pirates do not leave their signature in the destruction levels we encounter. To obtain some kind of starting point,
we necessarily must turn to textual evidence and later historical parallels and see if these can help us understand
the Bronze Age evidence. As to the first, one cannot avoid noticing the almost honorable regard for sea raiders
expressed in Homer, where most of the heroes commit acts of what we today would call piracy almost as a past

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
time, while busy laying siege at Troy (de Souza 1992). To kill time and to feed their armies, they take their boats
and grab whatever they can in the region, women especially. But Homer is also careful not to call his heroes
pirates (even if Thucydides does), while other, lesser folk and foreigners, are given the label, even if there is no
difference between their actions. Strictly speaking, however, and despite the use of the terms leistes and peirates,
one can question whether real piracy is in fact mentioned in the epics, since the term usually implies persons
who attack and rob ships at sea.
     Where the Bronze Age is concerned, we should also ask whether there was a fundamental difference ­between
what we now consider as acts of piracy and those committed by regular warriors or armies. The Mycenae silver
siege rhyton, for example, illustrates how one or more ships moored and a city was attacked (Papadopoulos
2019), and a very similar representation is preserved on a stone vase from Epidaurus, which, besides a boat
scene and a land raid, also includes a drowning person (Koehl 2006, 53, 185, 360, n. 818–19). Pirates or heroes?
If a pharaoh has his armies attacking a Levantine city, is this regular warfare, while if one city sends a ship to
pillage another city would this be piracy? The distinction is difficult to make and more a matter of appreciation.
Many scholars have tried to define piracy (e.g., Samaras 2015, this volume; Emanuel 2018) but, as far as the
­Aegean Bronze Age is concerned, Homer’s uncertainty is probably close to the truth. So, Thucydides (1.1.5) is to
 be forgiven when claiming that “no disgrace being yet attached to such an achievement, but even some glory”.

But how can we identify pirates and piracy in the Aegean Bronze Age. Pirate expert Marcus Rediker (1987,
257–58) already recognized three essential elements that large-scale piracy needed to fulfil: (1) pirates tend
to blossom in anarchic regions that border crucial sea lanes; (2) pirates tend to exploit established maritime
­networks to prey on passing commerce, and (3) since randomly seized cargoes do not always contain foodstuffs
 essential for survival, pirates need a “nest”, that is, a nearby friendly community where they can trade their
 plundered cargoes for everyday essentials without consequence and stock up on water. This definition is quite
 revealing as it comprises several features that may be archaeologically relevant (also Rediker 2004, 2014).
     The first is that piracy thrives in anarchic regions, as it did in the late 17th century, which should imply
that when strong authorities are present, piracy would be limited. It is such a situation already alluded at by
­Thucydides when stating that King Minos suppressed piracy while installing a sea-based hegemony. Leaving
 aside whether this was just a way of introducing Athenian naval policy, there are plenty of historical parallels for
 this: the Barbary pirates were only suppressed when France took control of North Africa in the 1830s, soon after
 the First Barbary War of 1801–1805 (Martin and Weiss 2019; de Lange 2021), more or less at the same time the
 US and European nations suppressed it in the Caribbean (Wilson 2021). This criterion would hence imply that
 we should concentrate on periods without a sufficiently strong political force in the Bronze Age Aegean to look
 for pirate activities. This is not an easy task either, since a strong land-based authority does not always possess
 a navy to act in tandem. Pharaonic Egypt, for example, only invested into an oceangoing navy during the New
 Kingdom (Emanuel 2021) and there is literary evidence that Keftiou ships docked at the harbor of Peru-nefer
 (Bietak 2010). The absence of a strong authority after the fall of the Minoan and Mycenaean palaces is often
 invoked as evidently giving rise to pirate activities during the Late Bronze Age (LBA) and continuing till the
 Archaic period (esp. Hitchcock and Maeir 2018). Whether Crete or some Cretan power actually was responsible
 for suppressing pirate acts during the heydays of Minoan culture remains, therefore, a possibility. The fact that
 coastal Cretan cities do not seem to pay special attention to defensive structures could also suggest that the seas
 were safe and that no attacks were expected from that side, but I will return to this below.
   A second important criterion is the existence of crucial sea lanes through which essential trade passed ­(Arnaud
2005; 2020). Sea currents are different in summer and winter, but one assumes that most piracy would take place
during the sailing months. 4th century CE Vegetius states that sailing in the Mediterranean was ­dangerous after

view). This said, the south coast of Crete is to be avoided during summer, since the mountains give rise to what
are called katabatic squalls, a wind that carries high-density air from higher elevations down a slope under the

witnessed before reaching Kaloi Limenes (Spratt 1865, 11–12; Mourtzas and Kolaiti 2021; Curtis 2023 ; Fig.
1). ­Furthermore, as Cristoforo Buondelmonti already noticed, this coast could only be navigated by crews that
knew the topography (Pryor 2006). But even the north coast was often avoided due to the strong meltemi winds,
and, during the Crusades, ships going east would prefer to travel from the Ionian Sea close to the Peloponnese
and hence through the Cyclades and the Dodecanese, with Crete being avoided (Arnaud 2020). Trading ships
would only approach Cretan shores if they were to board one of the major coastal towns, which, in the Bronze
Age, would have been Chania, Poros or Amnissos and a few other places along the north coast that offer suffi-
cient shelter, such as Souda Bay, the Spinalonga lagoon or Siteia. The north coast of Crete was, in any case, out
of the question during winter because of the fierce winds, and still today there are days, even in summer, when
the winds are so strong that even the big ships cannot sail. But with good winds, Egypt could be reached in just
four days (Kopanias 2017, 125).
    A third criterion is the existence of a thriving maritime network, and Carl Knappett and colleagues (2008;
2011) have extensively published on this. They have concentrated on the main phases of Minoan trade and
illustrate changes caused by the disappearance of Santorini-Akrotiri. In general, the links they highlight testify
to the dynamism of interaction during the Middle (MBA) and early LBA, but the advanced LBA could do with
some more attention despite some initial attempts by Tom Tartaron (2013), Francesco Iacono (2019), and Alex
Knodell (2021).
   Lastly, pirates need a free haven, a place that offers safety but also access to food and fresh water. One may
assume that such pirate’s nests would reasonably be at some distance from these sea lanes to avoid detection.
Where do we need to look and what are we specifically looking for? Small, off-shore islands were probably
quite popular – Gavdos, for example, was known as a pirate refuge, even used by Barbarossa as his base one
time ­(Kopaka and Kossyva 1999). The islands of Dia (Vokotopoulos, this volume) and pre-Venetian Spinalonga
could be others. Pseira island with its Minoan site would in fact be a good candidate as a pirate settlement.
­Mochlos too, with its original double harbor hidden by the island itself, could well have been a settlement with a

has many such caves that are immediately accessible from the sea. Hidden coves (e.g., Calypso or Pirate’s Cove
near Plakias, or Martsalos beach near the Ayio Farango gorge) and inlets of Crete provided ideal hiding spots
for pirates, and the further away from a major coastal settlement that had sufficient authority, the easier it was
for freebooters. Small, hidden creeks, such as those at Sissi, used to launch attacks against the Ottomans, that of
Ayios Nikolaos or Cape Sidero would have been ideal to hide before preying on passing ships.
     Why pirates do what they do is perhaps a redundant question and both Sahlins (1965) and Renfrew (1975)
have stressed how piracy is a form of negative reciprocity, an attempt to maximize personal gain from the
­transaction. Perhaps we could call it also a form of direct access, get things where you can directly, without
 paying or giving something in exchange. For the Bronze Age, we will never know whether the exotica and
 wealth in the different settlement or funerary contexts we encounter are the result of pirate activity. The eclectic
 nature of the Griffin Warrior’s assemblage at Pylos (Davis and Stocker 2022, 64, 83–4) does not rule out that
 this gentleman was occupied with less than honorable activities and the same may be true for other rich, but
 eclectic Mycenaean tombs in unexpected locations, as that on Skopelos, which, besides a marvelous long sword
 with gold foil decoration, also yielded a knife with duck’s head hilt, a spearhead, dagger and Late Helladic (LH)
 IIB Ephyraean goblets and alabastra (Platon 1949). I will come back to unusual wealth in otherwise mediocre
 archaeological contexts below.
     Apart from transmittable wealth, the epics and later historical sources inform us that people, and e­ specially
women, were sought after by pirates so that they could be sold as slaves. A study by Davis (2003; 2010) found
that, between the 16th and 19th centuries, more than a million Europeans were enslaved by Barbary pirates.
From the Linear B tablets, we learn of the presence of foreign women in the service of the palace at Pylos (Olsen
2014). Women from Knidos, Lemnos, Miletus and elsewhere were employed by the palace, usually in the ­textile
industry, and other women are explicitly called rawijaja, often translated as “captives”, hence announcing a
­passage in the Iliad where Achilles boasts of the women he captured in the area around Troy (Il. 20.193; see
 also Ergin 2007, 273). Slaves in general are mentioned in the Linear B records, but the references are relatively
 rare and slaves are always held by individuals, so I would not exaggerate official state acquisitions via piracy.
 Whether other elements, such as the terracotta spools used in textile production (Fig. 2) that show up regularly
 in Late Minoan (LM) and LH IIIA–C contexts, suggest the presence of foreign women, seems a reasonable sug-
 gestion (Driessen and Gaignerot-Driessen 2023), but we are unable to tell whether these women formed part
 of a larger population movement or whether they were captives, acquired during raids or bought in slave mar-
 kets from pirates. The oddity is that the prizes given at the Homeric funeral games –tripod basins and kraters,
 gold, horses, cattle, and women– are probably also those that were most prized by pirates. It is probably not a
 ­coincidence that Achilles brings out these prizes from his ships! (Il. 23.259; see especially Ready 2007).
     We even have less evidence when it comes to material traces of acts of piracy. That such things –attacking
and robbing ships at sea– were happening in the Bronze Age, is alluded at by the reference to Lukka pirates or
Misi in the Amarna letters (Emanuel 2020), and seems to be suggested by the scene on the north wall of the
­Flotilla Fresco of Akrotiri, Thera (Morgan 1988). This shows two main events: a seascene, usually dubbed the
 shipwreck scene, and a raid on land (Fig. 3). The first scene shows a captain with an outstretched arm and at least
 three nude people with a different hairstyle, drowning in front of his boat, and with them are floating shields
 and shepherd sticks, suggesting they may have been warriors. The nature of this scene is quite different from
 that on the opposite wall. Are these the ancestors of the Barbary pirates? Unfortunately, the scene is ­fragmentary
 so we cannot judge the nature of the ships involved nor whether the two partly preserved ships were manned
 by a crew similar to the drowning people. The second scene, the land raid, is immediately above this, so some
 connection can be assumed. Here, eight shield and spear carrying warriors with boar tusk ­helmets are heading
 inland and up the hill, where a dozen cattle are assembled, presumably to be taken away. The ­warriors are prob-
 ably the “good guys” but they are involved in what we may perhaps assume is piracy raiding. We can hypothesize

 gested. The flotilla scene in general and the many depictions of ships in Aegean and non-­Aegean iconography

­signature and thus it is difficult to blame pirates rather than another adversary for the destruction and pillaging
 of a settlement. A much-cited example is the Late Cycladic (LC) IIIC site of Koukounaries on Paros. Because
 of the discovery of bodies within the destruction layer, its excavator, Dimitrios Schilardi (1979; 1984), blamed

 2003). Each site in fact should be explored in detail: How did the destruction happen? Was it partial or ­complete?
 Pirates would, I think, rarely destroy a site entirely since it would be to their benefit if the settlement r­ ecovered
 so that it could be pillaged again. Bergen in Norway, for example, was pillaged by pirates in 1428, 1429 and 1432
 and although partly burned, enough was left to allow recovery (Stylegar et al. 2020).

without these being the result of trade? Or is there a concentration of unexplained wealth in modest coastal
settlements, like, for example, at Mochlos or even Petras? Such finds do not necessarily imply that these sites
themselves were pirate nests, but they may have provided safe havens for pirates to stock up and exchange valu-

which major state organizations were either absent or weakened, as in the Early Bronze Age (e.g., Yeagley
2022; Angelopoulou, this volume; Giagkoudaki, this volume) or, as is mostly the case, the advanced LBA (e.g.,
Samaras 2015). In their book “Pieces of Eight: More Archaeology of Piracy”, Ewen and Skowronek (2016, 279)
seek to answer whether it is possible to determine piratical behavior from recovered artifacts, deciding even-
tually that “the Golden Age of Piracy [in the 17th century Caribbean] may have been too short to leave a fully
developed pirate culture that is clearly recognizable in the archaeological record”, and this despite the length of
the period. This remark should also warn us from overinterpreting our evidence.

 Investigating the Origins of Piracy in the Aegean
Trade and Maritime Raids during the Early Bronze Age

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
During the Early Bronze Age II, the presence of imported raw materials, artifacts and technologies reveals an active
­exchange system and widespread maritime networks in the Aegean. Overseas contacts and the accumulation of wealth
 as the result of those practices changed the dynamics of society. Opportunities for economic benefits and social promotion
 became available, intensifying competition between those involved in maritime networks. The accumulation of wealth
 in the Aegean is usually interpreted as the result of intensive trade and gift exchange. At the same time, however, some
 scholars have argued that the distribution of exotic or valuable objects and raw materials may also have been the result of
 raiding, thus dating the origins of piracy to the Early Bronze Age II period. Other scholars dispute this view, arguing that
 there are fundamental differences that distinguish trade from raiding and warfare, and there can be no question of piracy
 in such an early period, while others accept the existence of piracy but claim that, in the absence of written sources, such
 activities cannot be documented, as their archaeological signature is weak.
This paper examines the possibility of the existence of piracy in the Early Bronze Age Aegean. For this purpose, the
­differences between piracy and war are discussed, and evidence of material culture possibly related to the phenomenon of
 piracy (e.g., ship technology and iconography, material culture and its use, settlement patterns and settlement features)
 are examined. It is argued that in such early societies there were no absolute distinctions between activities like trade,
 piracy, raids and war, and that these activities cannot be approached in a modern way of thinking. The evidence in the
 material culture may be indirect, but seems to suggest that piracy could have been practiced in the Early Bronze Age
 Aegean by the same people who participated in maritime trade and other “legal” activities.

2005, 339; Day et al. 2009, 335–37; Kouka 2014, 43–4).
    These maritime activities provided opportunities for wealth accumulation, which could be acquired either
by trading or raiding. The quite large number of fortified settlements and the destruction layers found in some
of them, the presence of weapons in settlement or burial contexts and the iconography of the period that in-
cludes ships and daggers, have led many scholars to accept the important role of raids in the EBA Aegean (e.g.,
Agouridis 1997, 20; Broodbank 2000, 253; Sherratt 2000, 135; Angelopoulou 2016–2017, 139–42).
    On the basis of the high maritime activity of the period and the positive correlation between trade and
piracy (see Samaras, this volume), this paper discusses the possible nature of the raids in the EBA Aegean and
attempts to investigate elements that may relate to the phenomenon of piracy during that period. Initially,
different views on piracy in the Aegean during the EBA are presented and discussed. Then, the motives of
pirate activity are explored, as derived from the possible perceptions, the iconography and the archaeological
evidence. Several aspects of the material culture of the EBA Aegean, e.g., the use of some objects and their sym-
bolisms, the changes in settlement patterns and the existence of settlements with strong defensive systems, offer
indications of potential pirate activities conducted by certain island communities.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Wealth accumulation in the Aegean was traditionally considered to be the result of intensive trade and/or gift
­exchange (e.g., Cherry 1981, 41–68; Cosmopoulos 1991, 155–67; Halstead and O’Shea 1992), so any influences
 or innovations observed in material culture were explained as a result of peaceful exchanges, while interpre-
 tations concerning the transfer of materials, people and technical knowledge by raiding or looting were only
 ­tentative or simply absent. At the same time, relevant studies have tended to emphasize the risks of sea travel,
  which were mainly attributed to weather conditions and the small capacity of ships of this period (e.g., ­Agouridis
  1997, 2–6; Broodbank 2000, 92–6), while the dangers from human hostile activity were ­underestimated, if not
  omitted, resulting in a somewhat one-sided approach to a complex phenomenon.
    Nevertheless, a small number of scholars has occasionally supported the possibility of pirate activity in the
EBA Aegean. Renfrew (1972, 440, 763) was probably the first to date the origins of piracy in the Aegean to the
EBA II, based on Thucydides’ claims (1.4.1) about unsafe navigation before the time of Minos due to pirates and
taking into account archaeological data, such as fortified settlements and the circulation of precious metals in
the Aegean. Renfrew’s opinion was accepted by Doumas (1988, 27–9) to explain the destruction at the end of
the Early Cycladic (EC) IIA in the northeastern Aegean and Asia Minor, and the east Aegean influences on the
material culture of the EBA IIB Aegean. He argued that “refugees-pirates”, following the familiar trade routes,
settled in major trading sites of the previous period, but also established new ones at key-points. This way, he
links trade with the conflicts and destruction that took place during this period and relates them to possible
pirate incidents. More recently new arguments have been added to the debate about the changes in the Aegean
during this period, adopting somewhat different interpretation and arguing that, beyond the movements of
people actively involved in sea trade, the spread of ideas, technical knowledge and objects may also be due to
conflicts and possible pirate activities (Yeagley 2022). Also, as discussed in more detail below, longboats of the
period have been suggested to be linked to piracy (Tzovaras 2020, 17).
    On the other hand, several scholars have presented counter-arguments to the above views that either have
to do with the existence of piracy in such an early period or with the (in)ability of the research to detect this
phenomenon. For example, Agouridis (1997, 20) argues that the archaeological footprint of piracy is similar
to that of trade, so no distinction can be made between these two activities. According to de Souza (1999, 2,
15), in periods without written sources piracy cannot be documented, as it leaves no archaeological footprint.
Moreover, it should be mentioned that Broodbank (2000, 410) denies the existence of piracy in the EBA Aegean,

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Despite the varying views in the debate on piracy, it seems generally accepted that maritime raids were ­conducted
in the EBA Aegean, so what should be investigated is the exact nature and purpose of these raids. Broodbank’s
objection to the recognition of these raids as pirate activities is mainly based on researchers attempting to
characterize the distant past using modern terms, perceptions and considerations. Indeed, in the EBA Aegean
there were no recognized rules equivalent to today’s maritime laws and therefore the legality or the illegality
of an action was not perceived in the same way. However, the A.P.Pir.A. project’s research about the history
of piracy reveals that pirates rarely described their activities as piracy and usually used arguments to “justify”
and “legalize” them. Also, it was very common for an action to be characterized as piracy in order to justify the
pursuit and punishment of certain people, regardless of whether they were really pirates or not and regardless
of the existence (or lack of) laws (see more in Samaras, this volume). Therefore, for a more secure approach and
understanding of the phenomenon of piracy, it seems that the characterization of an act as piracy should be
based on the examination of its objective parameters (such as, for example, means and motives) rather than on
how it was perceived and characterized by the people involved (perpetrators or victims) or whether there were
any recognized laws about maritime activity.
    Therefore, it seems necessary to investigate the nature of the maritime raids in the Aegean Sea and whether
these raids can be classified as piracy or be included in the scope of war, as it is undeniable that every war has an
economic-pillaging dimension, both in terms of motives (i.e., to boost the economy of a community or a group)
and in terms of results, as it is customary for the victors to pillage the losers. The boundaries bet

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
that the raids carried
out were organized and systematic and aimed at permanent results, such as the annexation of a territory or the
destruction of an economic rival. On the contrary, it is more likely that they were of small scale, carried out on
an occasional and perhaps opportunistic basis and were primarily motivated by the economic benefit of those
taking part in them. Therefore, and despite the aforementioned difficulties in distinguishing between piracy and
warfare, maritime raids in the EBA Cyclades seem to have been much closer to the characteristics of the former
than the latter.
     It should be also noted that the motive for a pirate raid may not have been only economic but also socio-po-
litical. The leaders of a community, by conducting a raid and risking themselves because of their participation
in such a dangerous action, which brought benefits to all community members, gained prestige and confirmed
and legitimized their social status within their own community. Considering the means of the period, the EBA
sea voyages were in themselves “heroic” acts, as one had to face the dangers caused by both sea and weather
conditions during travel and the resistance of the people under attack; an act could be even more “heroic”, when
the participants fought and the raiders returned with booty for the community.

with spoils. Moreover, the existence of coastal fortified settlements, the layers of destruction and the weapons
found in them, including sea pebbles used as slingshot projectiles (Angelopoulou 2016–2017, 139–41), lead us
to conclude that ship-to-settlement attacks probably took place.
    In conclusion, during the FN and EBA I, when sea voyages are increasing (Papadatos and Tomkins 2013,
355, 374), cargo boats appear to serve the trading needs and are likely to continue to be used in the following
period for the same purpose. As mentioned above, during the EBA II, maritime contacts intensified, causing
an increase in wealth in the Aegean, which acted as an attraction and could be acquired either by trading or
raiding. Since trade acts as a motive force for raiding, the emergence of the longboat in the period of trade
intensification is unlikely to be coincidental. During this period, the need for the construction of a new light,
maneuverable and fast ship suitable for raids seems to have arisen. In diachronic perspective, speed and maneu-
verability are the essential features of all pirate ships (e.g., see Nakas, this volume about the pirate ships in the
Classical and Hellenistic periods).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Since conditions and ships appropriate for pirate raids existed during the EBA, the question of the motives
for these raids inevitably arises. According to anthropological studies (e.g., Torres-Rouff and Costa Junqueira
2006, 60; Erdal and Erdal 2012, 78), social stress, resource constraints, and ecological problems (for example,
droughts and population decline), may lead to violent behavior such as raiding and looting. In the case of piracy
in the EBA Aegean, on which this paper is focused, the most obvious motive was the acquisition of valuable
objects and raw materials and as has already been mentioned, the enhanced social status of those who brought
them through such a “heroic” act. However, equally (or even more) valuable spoils may have been animals and
people, as they were necessary for the survival of a community, the former as a means of food and production,
the latter as a means of strengthening the human resource and reproduction through exogamy (Broodbank
2000, 86; Sherratt 2000, 135).
    In one of the rock-engravings from the Korphi t’Aroniou, for which it has been suggested that they date back
to the end of EC II or the beginning of EC III, an armed man leading an animal in a boat is depicted (Doumas
1965, 48–50; Fig. 1). Animals in ships are also represented in rock-engravings at Strophilas on Andros, which
date to the FN period (Televantou 2008, 47; 2009, 128; Fig. 2). These depictions are usually interpreted as the
movement of animals to smaller islands for grazing and/or breeding (Broodbank 1989, 332–33; 2000, 127–28;
see also Cherry 1985, 20), a practice still in use today in the Aegean (e.g., Chaniotis 1999, 191; Marketou 2023,
45).
     However, it should not be omitted that animals have always been included in pirate spoils and generally

practice confirms martial skills and brings social prestige, especially in societies that are accustomed to robbery
and piracy. Such scenes could therefore be depicted as a reminder of heroic achievements, like later hunting
scenes. The movement of flocks for grazing and/or breeding is an undeniable practice, but it is part of everyday
­activities, which are essential and necessary for survival, but do not carry the same social prestige and therefore

history of piracy reveals that the most common motives for the capture of persons were in obtaining ransom for
their release and enslavement for exploitation or sale. These two motives are extremely difficult to decipher in
the ΕΒΑ Cyclades, but the possibility of the abduction of women for reproduction cannot be excluded (Sherratt

Major changes in the settlement patterns and the ways of living are usually considered to be a result of the
­emergence of new needs and demands. In this regard, the abandonment of coastal sites and the move to fortified
 sites away from the sea are often attributed to threats and invasions from the sea. Therefore, a brief synopsis of
 the settlement patterns of the EΒΑ Cyclades and the identification of such changes may be able to contribute
 to the debate on the phenomenon of piracy during this period (see Angelopoulou, this volume for a more
 ­comprehensive discussion on the EC settlement patterns).
     The EC I settlements appear to be scattered and short-lived (Broodbank 2000, 150–51, 154–56; ­Angelopoulou
2016–2017, 134). They were small settlements, based mainly on the agricultural economy, while their external
contacts were limited. The settlements of the EC IIA period were also small in size and duration, with a few
­exceptions of larger and more organized settlements, such as Ayia Irini on Kea (Caskey 1971, 368–72; B­ roodbank
 2000, 216–18; see also Wilson 1999, 2013), Dhaskalio on Keros (Boyd 2013, Renfrew 2013), and Skarkos on Ios
 (Marthari 1997, 2008a, 2018). The settlements of this period were mainly coastal or near the sea and at nodal
 points of sea routes, indicating the interest of their inhabitants in sea voyages. There seems to have been some
 concern for protection from sea raids, by choosing either defensible sites, as in the case of Dhaskalio, or sites
 at a short distance from the sea, as at Skarkos (Broodbank 2000, 212–21; Angelopoulou 2016–2017, 134–35).
      An even stronger concern for protection from the sea emerged in the following EC IIB period. Several
­settlements were now situated on defensible hilltops, and many of them were reinforced by strong fortification
 walls. For example, settlements like Kastri on Syros (Marthari 1998, 2017), Panormos on Naxos (Angelopoulou
 2014, 67–88), Kynthos on Delos (MacGillivray 1980) and Markiani on Amorgos (Marangou 2006, 81–93)
 ­indicate feelings of danger and insecurity. Kastri and Panormos were indeed destroyed and then abandoned,
  probably after a maritime raid. This change in the settlement pattern from sites near the sea to defensible sites on
  high and steep hills and with strong fortification walls, combined with the evidence of attack, destruction and
  abandonment observed in at least two settlements, are indications of the fear during this period and the violent
  raids that seem to have come from the sea.

adequately explained by other “legal” activities (see also Samaras 2015, 191–92).

been witnessed in the FN period and the EBA I, as can be seen at Strophilas on Andros (Televantou 2006, 2008,

this theme, making the ship a symbol of the community and revealing its naval orientation. Several metal
objects have also been found in the same settlement, including a metal spearhead, while in Vathy there are
rock-­engravings of a unique theme with daggers, symbols of bravery and heroism indicating violent actions.
Considering that material culture is a powerful means of social display, it may be possible to accept the view that
ships transmitted messages of collective power and weapons that of individual power.
