findings.evidence_excerpt:
The geomorphology of Lefkada and the Inner Ionian Archipelago, with their rugged coastlines, intricate network of
­islands, and strategic location along important trade routes, have significantly impacted the region’s maritime history. The
 ­prevalence of piracy has also left some traces on these islands. The recent discovery of Late Helladic t­ umuli, a ­fortification
  wall and a prehistoric settlement at Meganisi has shed new light on the Taphians mentioned by Homer. According to
  legend, the Taphians were renowned for their seafaring skills and piracy. The discovery of these a­ rchaeological sites
  ­provides important new insights into the Taphians’ way of life and the extent of their influence in the region.
Written sources suggest the constant presence of pirates in the Ionian Sea, which posed a serious threat to trade. The
ancient ports played an essential role in the region’s maritime history, and there must have been numerous hideouts for
pirates in the broader network of the small islands like Atokos, Arkoudi, Echinades, Kythros, Kastos and Kalamos. The
long-standing presence of pirates in the restless waters of the central Ionian Sea is well-documented since the castle of Ayia
Mavra in Lefkada became an infamous pirate’s nest during early modern times.

Piracy, which can be defined as armed robbery involving the use of ships (de Souza 1999, 1), has been a ­pervasive
issue throughout history, and the ancient world was no exception. Greece and the Eastern Mediterranean Sea
were hotspots of piracy in antiquity, and it is a topic that has captivated scholars and historians for centuries
(e.g., Gabbert 1986; Ormerod 1924; de Souza 1999; Beek 2006; Konstam 2008; Emilio-Ioannidou 2017).
     This paper seeks to explore the evolution of piracy in the broader region of Lefkada, the Inner Ionian
­Archipelago, Echinades islands and the opposite Akarnanian coast, with an emphasis on the prehistoric times.
 Our finds strongly support the research regarding piracy in the Mediterranean Sea and more specifically in
 the Aegean during prehistory (see for example Hitchcock and Maeir 2018). The strategic position of Lefkada
 along crucial maritime trade routes, the geomorphology of Meganisi with its lace-like shores, and the com-
 plex network of small islands in the Inner Ionian Archipelago have significantly influenced the maritime his-
 tory of the broader region. Given the potential impact of piracy on these islands, there is a possibility that

findings.evidence_excerpt:
The Homeric poems constitute the earliest extant literary works depicting individuals and groups as pirates
(Od. 16.424–430). While the poems express a measure of disapproval for piracy, they simultaneously illustrate
the potential for a pirate to attain a higher social status through successful marauding. In essence, piracy was
not regarded as intrinsically ignominious or objectionable in the Homeric world, reflecting the socio-cultural
milieu of Homer’s Greece. Furthermore, piracy and warfare were so inextricably intertwined in the Homeric
universe that they were virtually indistinguishable.
    Meganisi, situated east of Lefkada, occupies a maritime area amidst the western coast of Akarnania and
the islands of Lefkada, Ithaca and Kephalonia. Within this region, numerous small islands and islets form the
Teleboides and Echinades island groups. Meganisi, belonging to the Teleboides group, is commonly identified
by scholars as the island referred to as Taphos in ancient texts (Od. 1.105, 1.181, 1.417–419, 14.453, 15.427,
16.426; Strabo 10.2.14, 10.2.20, 10.2.24). According to the Homeric tradition, this island served as a homeland
for pirates and traders. The name itself suggests that it may have been associated with tombs. In the epic poems,
capes and small islands positioned along sea passages were often linked to hero worship due to the proximity of
heroic deaths (for example, Ajax Lokros in Mykonos, Leukos in Lefkada, and according to Homer, the tomb of
Achilles in the Black Sea was visible to seafarers).
    The Taphians are considered Leleges or Phoenicians, who arrived in the region with Cadmus from the East.
Their main occupation seems to have been piracy in the southern Ionian region, as was the case with most tribes
of the Leleges, who were settled in other coastal areas and were usually mentioned in tradition as formidable
pirates (Vikatou 2019, 76–7).
    Although only the Taphians are mentioned in the Homeric epics, in later writers they are associated with the
Teleboans, another Lelegian tribe. According to Strabo (10.2.14, 10.2.20, 10.2.24), the Teleboans preceded the
Taphians. Both tribes inhabited the coastal cities of Akarnania and, after being displaced by the K
                                                                                                  ­ ephalenians,
settled on the neighboring islands of Akarnania, primarily Taphos, which is located between Ithaca and Lefkada.
However, it is possible that they represent the same tribe, initially known as the Teleboans and later as the
­Taphians (Vikatou 2019).
    The first references to the Taphians can be found in the Homeric epics. In the Odyssey, they are portrayed as
neighboring people of Odysseus’ kingdom, who, apart from being pirates, were also skilled traders, traversing
the Mediterranean Sea and competing even with the Phoenicians. In Book 1 (180–184), the king of the Taphians
Mentes, the son of wise Anchialos and a friend of Odysseus, is mentioned. He travels to the city of Temese to
exchange iron for copper. The epithet φιλήρετμοι, used by Mentes himself to describe his people, demonstrates
that they were renowned rowers, indicating furthermore that they were a seafaring nation. Additionally, the
term ὰλλόθροοι, meaning “speaking a different language”, implies their commercial activities with other people
of the Mediterranean. In other parts of the Odyssey, the Taphians are referred to as ληΐστορες (15.427, 16.426;
see also 14.452), indicating their piratical and plundering nature, as well as their involvement in the slave trade.
Specifically mentioned is their abduction of a slave woman from the city of Sidon in Phoenicia (15.425–429).
    In short, ancient sources offer indefinite testimonies regarding the Taphians-Teleboans and the islands they
inhabited (see Vikatou 2019, 79). Among other information, we learn that the island of Taphos derived its name
from the heroic first king of the seafaring Taphians, Taphios, brother of Teleboas. Later, Pterelaos, Taphios’ son,
extended his power to the surrounding islands and Kephalonia came under his rule. Its first inhabitants were
named Taphians or Teleboans. The small islands of Kastos, Sparti, Skorpios, Meganisi, Kalamos, etc., located

or Teleboan Islands.
    The mystery surrounding the people of Taphians and the exact location of the island is not easy to clarify, as
the ambiguity observed in Homer and the limited amount of information regarding their origin and ancestry
led to confusion and the formulation of many different opinions by later writers, including ancient ones (such
as Strabo, Pliny the Elder, etc.). As a result, the search for Ithaca naturally prompted efforts to identify Taphos.
Current research on the Homeric Taphos remains uncertain, with some scholars suggesting its placement in
Kephalonia, where a region named Taphios exists, while others propose Meganisi or Kalamos as potential loca-
tions (see Vikatou 2019, 83–4). However, from the entirety of the testimonies, it is inferred that the Taphians,
a piratical and trading people, dominated the Ionian Sea during the Mycenaean period, before the rise of the
Kephalenians, when they constituted a powerful naval kingdom. According to myths, they did not hesitate to
campaign against the Mycenaeans themselves, and they not only faced the powerful forces of that time but also
required trickery to be defeated (see Vikatou 2019, 76).

findings.evidence_excerpt:
The activity of pirates continued unabated, even after prehistoric times, in the broader area of the Ionian and
Adriatic Seas, where Greeks, Etruscans, Liburnians and other pirates ravaged the islands and coastal regions
(especially for the Liburnian pirates see Budić, this volume). Thucydides (1.5.3) mentions the Ozolian Locrians,
the Aitolians and the Akarnanians as peoples engaged in maritime piracy. He provides insights into the various
factions and activities during the war. One aspect he highlights is the prevalence of piracy in the region.
    Establishing colonies along the coasts of the Ionian Sea, which provided safe harbors, was an essential step
in combating the phenomenon of piracy that flourished from the shores of Zakynthos to Illyria. In the colony
of Lefkada, the Corinthians built the canal, which, especially during times of war, offered an alternative route
for a peaceful journey away from the dangerous promontory of Lefkatas in the southern part of the island
­(Rontogiannis 1988, 92–3; Zachos and Douzougli 2003; Bonelou 2020, esp. 82–6).
     In the present coastal zone of the settlement of Lygia, the large harbor of the island was constructed,
­protected by a substantia

 in the Ionian Sea, the excavations in this area bring to light “exotic” products that arrived on the island from all
 over the Mediterranean, due to the existence of extensive commercial networks (Filis and Staikou 2022, 270–74;
 Staikou 2023).
     On the northeastern side of the island, close to the harbor, the sanctuary of Aphrodite Limenida (or
­Limenarchis) is noted (Melfi 2016, 90–3), the precise location of which archaeologists have not yet been able
 to ascertain. Facing the goddess of the sea, the mariners would pray for safe journeys without storms and,
 ­evidently, without any encounters with pirates!
     The Messenian sculptor Damophon was called to Lefkada to repair the statue of Aphrodite Limenida (Melfi
2016, 90–8). An honorary decree inscribed on a monumental Doric column found in the Asklepieion of a­ ncient
Messene states that the people of Lefkada provided a rowing ship and many men for the protection of the
­Messenian sculptor during his return from Lefkada to the port of Kyparissia (IG IX.12 iv 1475). We can assume
 that the waters of the southern Ionian were not particularly safe during the 2nd century BCE, but as gradually
 over the next centuries the Romans imposed their forces in the Eastern Mediterranean basin (Etruria, Sicily,
 Illyria, Ionian Sea), and thus the pirates might have begun to lose their bases (Semple 1916, 143–44).
    Later on, from the early 16th to the late 17th century, the castle of Ayia Mavra, on the northeast edge of
Lefkada (Fig. 5), became one of the most famous pirate dens in the Adriatic Sea, as noted in the travel book
of Evliya Çelebi (Sarigiannis 2011, 50–1; Vikatou and Staikou 2023a, 22–3). The crews, consisting of renegade
Christians and Muslim sailors of Anatolian or even North African origin, were conscripted by the Ottoman ad-
ministration of the castle to assist the Ottoman fleet in maintaining control over the wider maritime area under
the rule of the Ottoman Empire. The pirate ship’s captain, who held the title of hâssa reis, was designated as the
legitimate leader of the other pirates of Ayia Mavra (Sarigiannis 2011, 57). Their targets were passing Venetian
merchant ships and the neighboring Venetian territories of Kephalonia and Zakynthos.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
The provocative actions of the pirates led to a counterattack by Maltese knights in May 1625 (Krantonelli
1991, 325). The corsairs arrived outside the fortress of Ayia Mavra with nine ships, blew up the eastern gate with
explosives, and climbed the walls using ladders. A prolonged confrontation followed, with casualties on both
sides.
     Considering the resurgence of piracy, on August 15, 1658, the Venetians attempted to capture the
­Turkish-held castle with Admiral Biki leading the operation (Vikatou and Staikou 2023a, 23). Pope Alexander
 VII supported the endeavor by sending three warships, while the Knights of Malta also participated. A general
 attack commenced after troops were disembarked in the neighborhoods surrounding the castle. However, the
 allies lost the element of surprise as they arrived in front of the castle walls during daylight due to bad weather.
 Furthermore, their coordination was inadequate, and they did not act swiftly. Thus, when they tried to climb
 the walls with the ladders they had brought, they discovered they were too short. Despite their attempts to
 blow up the fortress gate with explosives, they ultimately failed. After these mishaps, Admiral Biki was forced
 to order a retreat just a few hours after the operation began. Following the collapse of the Venetian Republic
 in 1797 and the presence of the French, Russian, and British on the island of Lefkada, Greeks and foreigners
 intermittently engaged in piracy or attacked ships of opposing naval forces (Çoruh 2018). The western coasts of
 Lefkada, particularly around Gria Langada, were a hotspot for renowned pirates until the early 19th century. In
 fact, their descendants have erected a –still standing– monument by the Pefkoulia beach to immortalize their
 legacy (Fig. 6).

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Throughout time, pirates in the central Ionian Sea would seek hideouts to avoid detection and launch s­ urprise
attacks on passing ships. The small natural harbors and bays along the islands’ rocky shores provided con-
cealment points suitable for ambush. At the same time, the intricate network of maritime passages offered
­alternative escape routes in case of pursuit.
    According to Dörpfeld’s theory (Dörpfeld 1927, 117–19) that Homeric Ithaca is identified with Lefkada and
considering the significant prehistoric settlement he found in the Nydri plain, he identified the sheltered bay
of Vlycho, near Nydri, as the primary harbor of Odysseus’ kingdom (see also Vikatou 2014, 10–1). The Vlycho
harbor is characterized by its depth, substantial horizontal expanse, and effective protection provided by the
cape of Ayia Kyriaki. Employing the same rationale, Dörpfeld (1927, 123–24) identified a small harbor at the
base of Mount Skaros, where the Dimosari stream meets the sea, as the location of Rheithron harbor (Od. 1.186).
From there, a commanding view towards the Pringiponisia is secured (meaning the cluster of small islands,
including Cheloni, Sparti, Skorpidi, Skorpios, Tsokari and Madouri). Finally, the harbor of Phorcys –where the
Phaeacians disembarked the sleeping Odysseus (Od. 13.116–124)– corresponds, according to the German ex-
cavator (Dörpfeld 1927, 109–13), to the present-day Syvota. The topographical details described in the Odyssey
(13.96–125, 13.345–351) are consistent: a small, enclosed, deep bay with sources of brackish water, large and
small caves around, at a remote location on the island.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
In the northern part of Meganisi, there is a noticeable fragmentation of the coastline, leading to the creation
of five large bays (Spilia, Vathy, Bali, Ambelaki and Atherinou), as well as numerous small ones resembling
fjords. Coves and natural moorages form in this area and in other parts of the island, providing ideal settings for
pirate activities. Today, only a limited amount of ancient construction material is preserved in Vathy, which can
be associated with the remains of the ancient harbor (Palmos 1992).
     The marine Papanikolis cave, located in the southwestern part of Meganisi, was undoubtedly used for
­thousands of years by ancient sailors who sought refuge in this shelter to protect themselves from storms or to
 hide. Its length is 120 m, the width varies from 60 m near the entrance to 23 m inside the cave, and its depth
 is approximately 30 m. It is large enough for ships, even those with relatively tall masts. It was named after the
 submarine Papanikolis, as it is said to have used the cave as a base during World War II, although this is more
 of a myth than a reality.
     The islets of Kythros and Atokos, characterized by their rocky coastlines, coupled with their relatively
­secluded locations, could have served as optimal natural hideouts for pirate vessels. Of particular interest is
 the islet of Arkoudi, situated south of Lefkada. Dörpfeld (1927, 98–101) associated this islet with the Homeric
 islet Asteris, where Telemachus sought refuge while being pursued by the suitors. Noteworthy are the islet’s two
 similarly configured harbors, as described in the Homeric narrative (Od. 4.844–847, trans. J.E. Huddleston,
 https://topostext.org/work/3):

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Closer to the coasts of Akarnania are the islets of Kastos and Kalamos, which feature secluded bays and
anchorages that would be attractive to pirates. In the central-western part of Kastos, there is a natural harbor
called Sarakiniko, facing north. Today, this name can be found in many coastal areas in Greece, where, as it is
said, Saracen pirates passed by and left their mark. In the Ionian Sea, the toponym Sarakiniko is also found in
Kephalonia, Ithaca and Preveza.
    Kalamos is the second-largest island in the Teleboan complex after Meganisi, resembling a lush mountain
in the heart of the Inner Ionian Archipelago (Μοutzali 2003, 71–6). Dörpfeld (1927, 134–35) believed that Ka-
lamos was the ancient Taphos, as the iron traded by the Taphian king Mentes (Od. 1.184) was not found on Me-
ganisi, but was abundant on Kalamos. The Porto Leone Bay, as named by the Venetians, who mapped the area,
could have been an ideal refuge for pirate ships throughout antiquity due to its adequate horizontal expanse.
Nowadays, at the bay’s entrance architectural material of the Venetian period is still visible (Fig. 7).
   Further south, the labyrinthine sea passages and small hidden coves among the islands of the Echinades
could have served as excellent locations for pirates attempting raids in Akarnania. In Platygiali, on the western
coast of Akarnania, facing the Echinades complex, an Early Bronze Age cluster of buildings has been excavated
underwater in the past. The tidally washed settlement inside the deep bay probably had a maritime character
(Delaporta and Spondylis 1991, 45).
    It is essential to delve into the profound significance of caves concerning pirate activity, particularly within
the karstic region of the Ionian islands and the shores of Akarnania. These areas boast a plethora of expan-
sive caves (Chirotrypa at Apolpaina, Chirospilia at Evgiros, the Cyclops’ cave in Meganisi, Chirospilia at Nea
Plaghia, to name a few) that probably could offer refuge to local inhabitants when confronted with the immi-
nent threat of marauding pirates prowling the coastal waters.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
The Liburnians, native people who lived along the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, are in ancient written sources
­frequently associated with piracy. Based on Strabo’s (6.2.4) and Appian’s (B Civ. 2.6.39) accounts of their presence on
 Korkyra and Epidamnos, scholars have developed the concept of the Early Iron Age Liburnian thalassocracy (ca. 800–
 500/400 BCE). Numerous historical interpretations have tried to strengthen or dispute the extent, scale, frequency and
 chronological scope of Liburnian influence and piracy. Through the analysis of regional geographical, economic and social
 circumstances, this paper aims to reconsider the concept of thalassocracy and give the explanatory tool for understanding
 Liburnian inclination to piracy.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
In the scholarly literature, historical accounts are frequently reinforced with archaeological details in an attempt
to support the Liburnian piracy narrative. For the authors who claim that intercepting and engaging with enemy
ships had been an integral part of Liburnian routine, rare and valuable objects, such as the helmet from the Cape
Jablanac on the island of Cres dated between 550 and 400 BCE, serve as a tempting proof for crimes on the sea
(Boršić et al. 2021, 21–2). In the light of Strabo’s (6.2.4) and Appian’s (B Civ. 2.6.39) accounts of the Liburnian
maritime dominance during the EIA in the south Adriatic and north Ionian Seas, scholars observe some for-
eign objects, particularly ones of Greek origin, as a possible outcome of sea raids. No wonder, piracy has been
highlighted as the probable way of acquiring Middle and Late Corinthian or Italo-Corinthian vases found on
the eastern Adriatic coast (Zaninović 2015, 86, 147). Nevertheless, this hypothesis deserves to be observed more
closely, due to many social and economic factors regarding the current state of archaeological research and the
knowledge about the EIA exchange networks in the Adriatic Sea.
    Firstly, the number of Liburnian sites containing Archaic or Early Classical Greek material is not abundant
(Šešelj 2009, 412–39; Čelhar and Borzić 2016, 78; Budić 2022, 62–4). Since many locations have not yet been
properly explored or excavated, it would be overambitious to conclude that valuable Greek objects scarcely
reached the Liburnian communities, and hence could be defined as potential spoils of occasional piratical raids
as Marin Zaninović (2015, 86, 147) suggested. The recent excavations in Zadar (ancient Iader) have exposed a
different pattern. Judged primarily on the size, location and political role of the site in later history (Čondić and
Vuković 2017, 32–3), Iader should be designated as the leading Liburnian hillfort and a strategic maritime hub.
The excavations in the Zadar old city, i.e., the former core of the Liburnian settlement, revealed a significant
number of imports, mostly of Daunian and Greek origin (Čondić and Vuković 2017, 74–99).
    Secondly, a discussion about the way foreign goods arrived among the Liburnians should not be observed
without insight into the trans-Adriatic prehistoric network, an often-overlooked phenomenon in the literature.
The circulation of the indigenous material shows a well-established pattern of exchange between the eastern and
the western Adriatic coast. During the EIA, Liburnian exchange with the opposite Italian coast is attested by
numerous imports, particularly from the region of Picenum and Daunia (Batović 1976; Majnarić-Pandžić 1998,

found on Liburnian sites (summary in Budić 2022, 365–68). Not only do their amount and spread reveal the
mechanism of the trans-Adriatic trade network, but also consequently challenge the hypothesis of the pre-
vailing EIA Liburnian thalassocracy in the Adriatic Sea. It seems far-fetched to define Liburnians as maritime
protagonists and the only ones responsible for dispersing the Daunian ware or similar circum-Adriatic material
along all its coasts (cf. De Juliis 1978, 20; D’Ercole 2002, 29). This argument can be further strengthened by
depictions of Novilara and Daunian stellae that uncover the maritime and possibly piratical character of the
western Adriatic peoples (Fig. 2; Staccioli 1983, 215; Nava 2004, 90–1; Medas 2016, 151, 160).
   Bearing in mind the trans-Adriatic exchange networks, the concept of the EIA Liburnian thalassocracy im-
mediately turns to the question of its validity. Even without the insight into archaeological material, historians
have warned about the issue of criticality towards Strabo’s (6.2.4) and Appian’s (B Civ. 2.6.39) testimonies (e.g.,
Džino 2014, 52–5; Barnett 2017, 74). In addition to Strabo’s narrative about the Liburnian presence on Korkyra,
ancient literature offers two different accounts. In a purely mythological context, Apollonius Rhodius (4.1211–
1216) wrote that the Colchians and the Phaeacians lived on the island prior to the Corinthian arrival. On the
other hand, Plutarch (Quaest. Graec. 11) claimed that Korkyra had been previously inhabited by the Euboean
Eretrians. Even though the archaeological research showed the predominance of the local Illyrian material on
Korkyra prior to the Greek arrival, the objects are not related to the Liburnian material culture (Malkin 1998,
78 n. 65). Moreover, not only is Appian’s narrative claimed to be anachronistically inserted (Čače 2002, 86–9),
but the EIA scope of Liburnian influence on the western Adriatic coast also remains doubtful (Čače 2002, 96–7;
D’Ercole 2002, 26–30; Džino 2014, 52–5; Barnett 2017, 74).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
During the second half of the 6th century BCE, Greeks founded two settlements in the northern Adriatic
­(Giudice et al. 2004, 178; D’Ercole 2007, 160 n. 5). Those were Adria and Spina, whose brisk economic success
 can be recognized by immense Attic imports during the 5th century BCE (Reusser et al. 2011, 105–6 n. 1),
 as well as by ancient written testimonies (Dion. Hal. Ant. Rom. 1.18.4; Strabo 5.1.7, 9.3.8). Judging from the
 current state of research, especially the lack of systematic archaeological knowledge of indigenous sites and the
 relatively limited number of Greek artifacts, it is only possible to assume that the establishment of new trade
 routes correlated with the increase in piratical activities (cf. Gabrielsen 2001, 220–21). However, it seems that
 the Greeks preferred to sail along the western coast or to follow the central Adriatic axis due to distance and
 sailing duration from northwestern Greece to the mouth of Po River (Kirigin et al. 2009, 149). Consequently,
 this would also keep them beyond the reach of the Liburnian, Histrian and Illyrian pirates, who lurked within
 the island zone of the eastern Adriatic.
    Soon after the establishment of Adria and Spina, Hecataeus of Miletus (6th/5th century BCE) compiled his
World Survey (Περίοδος γῆς), which contained the first known geographic and ethnographic description of the
eastern Adriatic coast. Although this work has been preserved only in fragments and there were undoubtedly
subsequent interventions by Stephanus Byzantius or some earlier authors (Billerbeck 2014, 217 n. 112), the
Liburnian ship highlighted there was not linked to any kind of piratical activities (FGrH I F93 = Steph Byz. s.v.
Λιβυρνοί). Stephanus Byzantius also draws attention to the Liburnian mandia (λιβυρνικὴ μανδύη), a garment
associated with the Liburnians. While it cannot be proven that Hecataeus’ account already contained this par-
ticular detail, especially given the fragmentary state of the tradition and the likelihood of later interventions, it
is nevertheless noteworthy that the same motif is attested in a fragment of Aeschylus’ lost tragedy (TGF F364).
The earliest surviving Greek testimony about the Liburnians, then, foregrounds an element of clothing rather
than any association with piracy.
     However, this argument does not necessarily allude to the fact that the Liburnians were not engaged in
­ iracy. If one considers the synchronous Greek attitude on the social acceptability of piracy as part of the
p
­everyday economy (for instance, Hdt. 3.39.3–4, 6.17.1; Thuc. 1.5.1–3), Hecataeus might not have needed to
 highlight piracy as a distinctive Liburnian feature. An identical concept and pattern could be applied to The
 Periplous, a more detailed geographical and ethnographic work written by Pseudo-Scylax around the mid-4th
 century BCE. In his pilot, the Liburnians were not brought into any connection to piracy (Ps.-Scyl. 21). The
 only testimony that is sometimes associated with piracy in literature belongs to logographer Lysias. In two of his
 speeches (32.25, fr. 1.4.40-41), Lysias pointed out the dangerous navigation in the Adriatic, but it is not possible
 to discern whether the reason for this was piracy, hazardous maritime and weather conditions, long-distance
 voyages or the combination of everything proposed.

The threat at sea that the Greeks experienced after colonizing the island of Pharos took the form of an organized
indigenous resistance (Suić 2003, 21), not a set of marginal pirate attacks. Diodorus further described that the
Greeks managed to suppress the native uprising by sinking and capturing their ships.
    New Greek settlements in central Dalmatia imply an increase in maritime traffic and therefore a greater
likelihood of maritime attacks. Several decades after the foundation of Issa and Pharos, Diodorus explicitly
highlighted indigenous piracy, while describing the establishment of two unnamed colonies around 360 BCE in
Apulia by the Syracusan tyrant Dionysius the Younger: “…the barbarians who dwelt along the coast were accus-
tomed to put out in numerous pirate ships and render the whole shore along the Adriatic Sea unsafe for merchants”
(Diod. Sic. 16.5.3, trans. C.H. Oldfather, Cambridge, Mass., 1933). Some scholars are inclined to connect this
account with the piracy of the eastern Adriatic people, who appear in Livy’s narrative (10.2.4) as infamous sea
raiders (Čače 2005, 173). Chronologically speaking, Cleonymus’ sailing venture in the Adriatic (302 BCE),
described by Titus Livius, took place only around 50 years after the establishment of Dionysius’ Apulian settle-

and the Etruscans, are often associated with piracy at that time (see Dell 1967, 354–56, with references to lit-

During the second half of the 3rd century BCE, the Roman interest in the eastern Adriatic coast commenced.
The simultaneous increase in maritime trade –confirmed by archaeological evidence (Šešelj 2009, 478–79)–
could have been followed by more intensive piratical activity (Gabrielsen 2001, 237; Čače 2013, 21). Livy (10.2.4)
placed the infamous piracy performed by the Illyrians, Histrians and Liburnians at the turn of the 3rd century
BCE. In other written sources (e.g., Polyb. 2.8.1; App. Ill. 1.3; Cass. Dio 12.19), maritime raids were frequently
noticed as a dominant indigenous feature and a logical cause for the Roman military reaction.
     However, the protagonists were not the Liburnians, but the Ardiei – an Illyrian tribe that dwelt south of
the Liburnian territory. Ardiei became notorious for their piracy during the reign of Queen Teuta in the 220s
BCE. Maybe it was not coincidental that the 2nd century CE Roman historian Florus equated the Illyrians to
the Liburnians, and confused them with the Ardiei. The common denominator could have been the m             ­ aritime
­domination: “The Illyrians, or Liburnians […] spread widely along the coast of the Adriatic Sea”, but more n ­ otably
 for their piracy blended with cruel crimes: “Under the rule of their queen Teutana, not content with ­depredations,
 they added crime to lawlessness. When our ambassadors came to protest against their delinquencies, they slew
 them, not with the sword, but like sacrificial victims, with the axe, and burnt to death the commanders of our ships”
 (Florus 1.21.1–4, trans. E.S. Forster, Cambridge, Mass., 1929).
    During the 2nd and the first half of the 1st century BCE, Liburnian piracy was almost completely omitted
from the written sources (for an overview, see Čače 2005, 173–74). The only direct mention is linked to ­Octavian’s
venture against the Liburnian pirates in 35 BCE (App. Ill. 4.16). Many scholars support the hypothesis of their
collaboration with the Roman side (Čače 1991, 59–62; 2005, 178; Zaninović 2015, 347; Milivojević 2017, 107–
8), while the Illyrians and Delmatae assumed the status of the most ferocious rivals. In addition, the analysis of
the archaeological material found along the eastern Adriatic sites suggests ongoing trade between Greeks and
Liburnians that flourished during the 3rd and the 2nd century BCE (Šešelj 2009, 513–27). Although the written
sources on the history of the eastern Adriatic Sea are scarce, the Liburnian pirate reputation is sporadically used
in scholarly literature as an explanatory tool for complementing the regional historical context. For instance,
Morgan (1973, 39–43) used that pattern to supplement the context of Gaius Sempronius Tuditanus’ campaign
during 129 BCE in Illyricum.

Having in mind a chronological overview and various interpretations, it looks apparent that a more detailed
­understanding of the Liburnian piracy extent, scale and chronological scope is gravely limited by various
 ­obstacles.
    Firstly, to interpret pirate raids exclusively on archaeological material appears to be misleading. Even a
small amount of exotic trade goods could always have diverse provenance backgrounds: direct or intermediary
exchange and trade, tribute, piracy and similar. It is also implausible to link the number of shipwreck finds
belonging to merchant cargo ships with local piracy patterns, since keeping captured vessels was crucial for the
transport of stolen goods. The presence of valuable commodities on shipwreck sites, especially an ample load
of amphorae carrying desirable liquids that ought to have been plundered, could be additional support to the
hypothesis (cf. Royal 2012, 440–41; Boršić et al. 2021, 23). However, a different scenario should not be excluded,
since there must have been instances of pirates sinking the captured ships and leaving the bulky cargo such as
amphorae aside, while stealing only luxurious objects and enslaving the crew (cf. Gabrielsen 2003, 394; Lewis
2019, 103). Based on the overall archaeological research conducted on the eastern Adriatic coast so far, there has

research on such locations is a significant barrier.
      Secondly, simply relying on written sources seems also deceptive. because they tend to highlight crucial
­historical episodes and omit marginal pirate attacks not related to major political events. The case of the pre-
 served records about the eastern Adriatic Sea completely fits into the picture. On top of that, authors who
 worked under the firm and well-established Roman influence, such as Diodorus Siculus (1st century BCE),
 Strabo (1st century BCE), Livy (1st century BCE/1st century CE), Appian (1st/2nd century CE) and Florus
 (2nd century CE), deliberately emphasized Liburnian piracy as an obstructive feature and frequently mentioned
 it in the context of former Greek or Roman territorial and maritime pretensions. Some of them undoubtedly
 reflect Roman anti-piracy measures. On the other hand, the absence of Liburnian sea raiders among earlier
 Greek writers can be understood as a reflection of the general acceptance of piracy as an omnipresent economic
 activity. Above all, one should never forget the survivorship bias when analyzing written sources. Therefore,
 their limited number, either due to the state of their preservation or due to marginality of the eastern Adriatic in
 ancient sources, should not serve as appropriate support for interpreting the extent and frequency of Liburnian
 pirate attacks.
   Several different thoughts have been put forward in the literature. Henry A. Ormerod (1924, 14) and ­Maurice
Holleaux (1952, 79–80) supported piracy as a general endemic habit or a local economic pattern of the eastern
Adriatic Sea. Although the hypothesis of endemic piracy is frequently repeated in scholarship (e.g., Bandelli
2004, 64; Fuscagni and Marcaccini 2004, 139; Prusac Lindhagen 2009, 77; Medas 2016, 144–45), it has recently
been criticized as well (Džino and Domić Kunić 2013, 81; Boršić et al. 2021, 23).
      A different theory tends to support periodic piratical activities depending on the level of trade ­cooperation
and political circumstances in the eastern Adriatic region. For instance, based solely on a study of the written
evidence, Harry J. Dell (1967, 354–55) concluded that the evidence for any early Illyrian piracy was tenuous.
­Although concentrated on the general picture, Dell (1967, 356) stated that the Illyrians, including the ­Liburnians,
 did not engage in serious high-seas piracy before 231 BCE. On the other hand, Slobodan Čače (2005, 176–77)
 claimed that during the Hellenistic period (3rd–1st centuries BCE) the Liburnians were collaborating with
 foreign merchants, so they must have worked on piracy prevention. According to his opinion (Čače 2005,
 180), the concept of Liburnian piracy is more a reflection of contemporary Greek and Roman prejudices, based
 on occasional conflicts in the maritime space after the establishment of Greek colonies in central Dalmatia.

massif on the mainland (Riđanović 2002, 191–92). Niches of numerous small islands or indented mainland
provide safe shelters for sailors in case of hazardous weather conditions (Fig. 4). However, they simultaneously
make a perfect setting for sudden sea raids. In addition, a well-indented coast requires a good local knowledge
of underwater topography (Morton 2001, 116). This could have been a great advantage for regional sea raiders,
as they could easily lure the victim into a trap. Although never directly linked to piracy in written accounts,
the Greek pilot books emphasize the vast number of islands along the eastern Adriatic coast. The Periplous
of Pseudo-Scylax (21–23) mostly lists various islands, pointing out their geographic position. However, the
most prominent example is Pseudo-Scymnus’ Periegesis (372–374), where the Liburnian islands, as well as the
Kvarner islands Apsyrtides and Electrides, are equated to the Cycladic archipelago – a convenient setting for
piratical raids as well (e.g., Ducrey 1983; Mendoni 2009).
     The lack of comments regarding piracy in these works can simply be explained by their genre. However,
when Livy described Cleonymus’ venture, he strictly differentiated the western from the eastern shore of the
Adriatic Sea – the first being harborless, the other notorious for piratical activities (10.2.4). Based on what
can be discerned from the geography, the crucial difference between them is a straight coastline on the west,
in c­ ontrast to a well-indented coast and dense archipelago on the east. Apart from the ancient pilot books,
­numerous eastern Adriatic islands were also emphasized by Apollonius Rhodius (4.524-575). His Argonautic
 expedition in the Adriatic Sea resembles a prospecting report, stressing the most important navigational land-
 marks. Among them were the islands that “lay thick and made the path dangerous for those who sailed thereby”.
 With those words, he described the realm of the Hylleans, who used to devise their hurt on the sea (Ap. Rhod.
 Argon 4.524–527, trans. R.C. Seaton, Cambridge, Mass., 1912). Geographical factors should indeed serve as a
 fundamental background for a regional piracy discussion.

Karst relief, which dominates northern Dalmatia and the Kvarner region, provides scarce terrain. The most
distinctive features are the fragmentation of fertile land, the dominance of smaller land patches, especially on
islands, the lack of longer and continuous surface streams and rivers, as well as a confined number of springs
on islands. In general, the eastern Adriatic Sea offers limited carrying capacities with a high probability of
­insufficient life resources (more detailed insight with bibliography in Budić 2022, 292–350). Another important
 economic factor is general shortage of metal supplies. Since karst relief lacks ore resources, for the regional
 market supply it was necessary to import raw material from distant areas (Budić 2022, 243–70). Consequently,
 the competition for metal might have been more pronounced in such circumstances, while piracy seems like
 one of the easiest ways to obtain it.
     All these arguments serve as a firm background for potential short or long-term shortages in the whole
region. The phenomenon could contribute to the idea of frequent pirate raids to strengthen the local economy
(cf. Dell 1967, 357), especially in a shelter of a well-indented coast, where raids could have been sudden, swift
and unexpected. This claim can be strengthened by Aristotle’s remark that pirates were just farmers who would
seasonally embark on raids to enlarge their income and avoid starvation during lean years (Pol. 1256b). For
instance, Strabo (11.2.12) directly attributed such a way of life to the Heniochoi, the Zygoi and the Achaei,
peoples who dwelt on the eastern coast of the Black Sea. They are described as part-time farmers, compelled to
till a poor soil, and part-time pirates. It should be kept in mind that not only foreign merchants should be seen
as victims of piracy; robberies at sea could have also taken place between various Liburnian communities. The
antagonism between them is known from Roman times (App. B Civ. 2.6.39; see also Roman epigraphic evidence
in Suić 1981, 107). There are also socio-political reasons why the idea should be taken into consideration for an
earlier period.

According to Irad Malkin (2002, 154), a maritime civilization implies a society that makes a living from the sea
and utilizes it as a gateway to distant shores. Geographical and economic conditions undoubtedly influenced the
development of Liburnian society. The coastal and island Liburnian communities were beyond the shadow of a
doubt maritime people, with sea playing a cardinal part of their economy, politics and everyday life. Therefore,
one can expect a maritime space monopolization, which could have been frequently carried out through piracy.
It is no wonder that a frequent Liburnian feature in historical accounts is the utility of their fast naval ships,
called liburnae or liburnicae (e.g., App. Ill. 4.16; B Civ. 2.6.39). The latter account directly linked them to pirate
expeditions against their neighbors.
    The maritime monopolization was probably carried out on the local level, since the society of Liburnia (a
territory between Raša and Krka Rivers) seems politically well-fragmented. Although for earlier periods this
can only be speculated, it should be noted that early Greek geographers mentioned numerous ethnonyms along
the area later ascribed to the Liburnian territory (cf. Plin. HN 3.139). Hecataeus of Miletus (FGrH I F94–96)
named Mentores, Syopioi and Hythmitai, while Pseudo-Scylax (21) listed many terms (such as Idassa, Attienites,
Dyurta, Haloupsoi, Olsoi, Pedetai and Hemionoi) that are difficult to determine precisely due to the corruption
of the text. Nevertheless, scholars mostly agree they should be understood as various Liburnian peoples, tribes
or settlements (the most accepted interpretation was brought by Suić 1955, 161; for a slightly different account,
see also Counillon 2006, 21–2, n. 14, 18). Pseudo-Scymnos (372–374) noted Ismenoi, Mentores and Pelago-
nians, and even Pliny the Elder (HN 3.139) reminiscently stated that the Mentores, Himani, ­Encheleae, Buni
(probably Bulini) and Peucetii (Peucetians) used to belong to the Liburnian race. Additionally, he emphasized
the internal Liburnian social division into fourteen separate communities. In the mythological context, Virgil

in the plural form. Although the concept of political unity among the Liburnians can sometimes be found in
the older scholarship (Suić 1981, 107–9; Čače 1985, 88, 677–91), it seems more reasonable to define it as a weak
socio-political alliance.
    Besides social fragmentation caused by local geography, predominantly based on karst terrain obstacles and
a labyrinth of numerous islands, there are no implications in the written records that Liburnians ever formed a
centralized state. The absence of regional or supra-regional central authority could consequently create anarchy
at sea, where there was no one to guarantee safety while trading or sailing. This could have been performed
through a set of local monopolies over maritime space that would include piracy as a means of surveillance,
control and display of dominance. Although not directly related to the Liburnians, a similar pattern appears in
the narrative of the 3rd century BCE, which testifies to the weakness of the regional central authority and its
repercussions realized through Illyrian piracy. Having received the Roman delegation, the Illyrian Queen Teuta
replied to the Roman envoys that it was not customary for the Illyrian kings to hinder their subjects from piracy
(Polyb. 2.8.8).
    Additionally, ancient writers pointed out gynecocracy and privileged female role as a prominent feature of
Liburnian society (Ps.-Scyl. 21; Nic. Dam., FGrH 90 F 103d; Varro, Rust. 2.10.8). This could be another reason
why Florus (1.21.1) equated the Liburnians and the Illyrians, since the latter were ruled by Queen Teuta at the
time. It is justifiable to debate whether to observe the Liburnian gynecocracy as fact, fiction or modus of Greek
and Roman mockery towards the “others”. Be that as it may, it seems that the prominent female role in the
Liburnian society should be seriously considered (e.g., Alföldy 1961, 318; Suić 1963, 54–5). Various maritime
activities would contribute to the long-lasting absence of men at home (cf. Alföldy 1961, 318–19; Kurilić 2008,
50). That would certainly include piracy as a lucrative activity. Moreover, such social trends would be an addi-
tional aggravating factor for social unification and centralization processes in the Liburnian society. Aristotle’s
comment (Pol. 1256b) on peasants who seasonally resorted to piracy helps to better understand such social
dynamics.
     Finally, ancient sources frequently stress that pirates sought to capture slaves (e.g., Hom. Od. 9.39–42,
14.262–265; Hdt. 3.39.3–4; for various inscriptions from Hellenistic period, see Mendoni 2009; Gabrielsen
2013, 147–48; Lewis 2019, 96–9; Pacheco 2020, 100–1). Pseudo-Sylax (23) briefly noted slavery within the
­Liburnian society. Unfortunately, due to a lack of more details, a more comprehensive insight into Liburnian
 slavery ­remains elusive. However, judging from historical context, it is reasonable to assume that one of the
 main sources of slaves in Liburnian society must have been piracy.

Although the Liburnians were not the only people in the Adriatic Sea labeled as vicious pirates, it should be
noted that by observing their coastal living space and environment, piracy seems as one of logical economic
pursuits. So far, scholars have emphasized the Greek and Roman demonization of Liburnians or the inventing
of piracy narratives, but it seems justified to presuppose a strong economic and social base for frequent sea
raids. The geographically fragmented territory with numerous islands acts as an appropriate scene for piratical
ventures. Regional economic conditions provided by the karst landscape, as well as social indicators based on
written sources, suggest that piracy was innate to the people who lived in such environment. It is no wonder
that seaborne raids are frequently attributed to the Histrians and the Illyrians, whose living space shared general
geographic and economic similarities.
    Neither historical sources nor archaeological finds can give a sufficiently clear understanding of Liburnian
piracy in terms of its frequency and chronological distinctiveness. Nevertheless, in the eastern Adriatic context,
all aforementioned circumstances suggest that piracy should be seen as a sort of endemic habit that implies

piratical opportunities at micro-locational levels. Not only does this include attacks on foreign merchant ships,
but also potential seaborne raids among Liburnians and other eastern Adriatic communities (cf. App. B Civ.
2.6.39) due to their spatial, social and political disunity. The competition for basic life resources in the austere
eastern Adriatic environment is an additional argument for the proposed hypothesis.
     On the other hand, interpreting the EIA Liburnian thalassocracy through the lenses of far-flung piracy along
the whole Adriatic should be observed with great caution. Primarily, a tradition on which the contemporary
Liburnian thalassocracy narrative was constructed seems to be a subsequent intervention done by the Roman
authors. This is furthermore supported by the exchange of goods between the eastern and western coasts of the
Adriatic Sea during the EIA, showing that the power relations at sea were polycentric. The Liburnians could not
have been the sole distributors of various circum-Adriatic goods, especially of Daunian pottery. To maintain a
good exchange balance, it would be difficult to imagine active Liburnian piracy along the whole Adriatic area.
Likewise, the extension of political power to Epidamnos and Korkyra does not get any support in the historical
or archaeological context. It seems more plausible that pirate activities were limited to the Liburnian ecosphere,
i.e., coastal belt marked by a highly indented coast, followed by a confined economic background and politically
fragmented society.
     Thus, we stand by Ormerod’s opinion (1924, 14–5) that specific geographic niches should be viewed as a
fertile area for piracy development. Some Mediterranean regions, such as Cilicia, Liguria and ultimately the
archipelago of the eastern Adriatic Sea, with Liburnia as its most indented part, had distinct predispositions and
it is not surprising they appear in historical sources as infamous for seaborne attacks (cf. Strab. 7.5.10). More-
over, regardless of continuities and discontinuities in material and written evidence, piracy had always been an
integral part of such an environment. Regarding the hypothesis about eastern Adriatic piracy as a reflection of
social transformation in the 4th century BCE, we support a different perspective. An insight into prehistoric
material reveals a vivid exchange network in the Adriatic Sea during the EIA. Hence, valuable imports must
have affected social differentiation even earlier, thus creating elites who tried to establish themselves within
their communities through trade and piracy.
     Liburnian piracy appears in ancient texts as a social feature. Therefore, its occasional appearance in written
sources should not be an indicator of a decrease or increase in the intensity and frequency of maritime attacks.
Since Greek historical accounts frequently reflect piracy as a legitimate economic activity, the lack of labeling
­Liburnians as notorious pirates in Greek sources should not stand as an argument for absence of sea raids.
 Moreover, there is a clear distinction regarding the Roman sources that exhibit the Mediterranean anti-piracy
 politics of the time. Due to the necessity to highlight such episodes, Liburnians appear in them as notorious sea
 raiders.
    By observing this framework from a broader historical perspective, Liburnian piracy and regional maritime
dominance seem to be valid arguments not only for creating the concept of the Eastern Adriatic as a dangerous
space from the Greek point of view (cf. Lys. 32.25, fr. 1.4.40–41), but also as a cause of a longer absence of
­permanent Greek settlements in the eastern Adriatic Sea, until the beginning of the 4th century BCE.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The Antikythera wreck is one of the most famous archaeological assemblages. During its last and fatal itinerary, the ship
departed arguably from Delos, in order to transfer its precious cargo to Italy. While it is usually assumed that the wreck
was caused by extreme weather conditions, in this paper we explore a different possibility. Once the wreck is viewed in its
topographical and historical context, several strange facts emerge. Most notably, the ship was discovered very close to the
pirate’s settlement of Aigilia and very far from its alleged route, through the Elaphonissos Strait. During the probable time
of the wreck, Rome was pursuing Crete’s subordination, under Metellus’ generalship, and at the same time the e­ mpire was
striving to clear the Mediterranean from piracy, under Pompey. This means that a ship serving Roman interests would
by all means have avoided sailing through an area controlled by Cretan pirates. Thus, we propose that the ship may have
been kidnapped by Aigilian pirates and hauled to their base for ransom. Such an action may have provoked Roman
­vengeance, given that Aigilia was attacked and obliterated, presumably in 67 BCE.

the 4th century BCE, as well as of a marble statue of Apollo, dating to the 2nd century BCE (Athens, National
Archaeological Museum inv. no. 230; Stais 1889, 238, 240–42; Flashar 1992, 85; Kaltsas 2002, 271, no. 567).
    Another structure that underlines the strong maritime character of the town is a shipshed. Located at the
west shore of the peninsula, beyond the confines of the harbor, the shipshed was carved into the rocky terrain
(Figs. 4–6). The shipshed has a total length of approximately 30 m, with a main compartment 18 m long, which
was used as the main shelter of the ship. It was also annexed by an autonomous, external compartment, a
“resting area” for a ship waiting to launch a piratical attack (Tsaravopoulos 2015, 28–9, fig. 11).
   Among the portable finds that were discovered in the settlement are numerous weapons and articles of
armor (Tsaravopoulos 2023). These include bronze and iron arrowheads, lead sling bullets of several types,
some of which are inscribed, catapult missiles and many wide-headed bronze nails with tiny relief lumps at the
inner side of the head, which were suitable for fastening the leather lining of shields (on this type of nails, see
Tsaravopoulos 2010–2013). Such finds are highly suggestive of a community in a state of fighting alert.
     Numismatic evidence, stamped amphora handles and inscribed sling bullets suggest that Aigilia was part
of the territory of Phalasarna on west Crete (Tsaravopoulos 2004–2009, 337–38; 2012, 210–11; on Phalasarna,
see Hadjidaki 1988, 2015 with earlier bibliography). All datable finds discovered thus far were dated from the
late 4th century BCE to the second quarter of the 1st century BCE; apparently, this period corresponds to the
lifespan of the settlement.

The limited productive capacities of Antikythera make it difficult to maintain a well-populated community,
let alone create sufficient surplus for the construction of monumental fortifications and other structures. This
reality raises a series of crucial questions regarding the historical circumstances under which the impressive
fortifications of Aigilia were built.
       A porous stone statue base that was discovered in 1888 at the harbor of Xeropotamos offers some ­valuable
clues (Stais 1889, 238, 240–42). An inscription on the base (IG V.1 948) gives the information that it was
­dedicated to Apollo of Aigilia by Aristomenes, son of Aristomedes, from the Thessalian Pherai. As Nick Sekunda
 has suggested (2004–2009, 597–99; see also Tsaravopoulos 2004–2009, 330–31), the reference to ­Aristomenes
 has far-reaching historical ramifications. A certain Aristomenes was a commander of the Persian fleet in the
 ­Aegean during the reign of Darius III (Curt. 4.1.36). On the other hand, one of his relations –probably his
  ­father– Aristomedes served as a general of the Persian army in the Battle of Issus (Arr. Anab. 2.13.2; Curt.
   3.9.3). The presence of an official of Aristomenes’ caliber on this small island is a striking fact. After the Battle of
   Granicus, the Persian authorities bought the alliance of several Cretan cities in an attempt to organize a counter­
   offensive against the back of Alexander’s III lines (for the evidence for the Persian counter-offensive see Burn
   1952, 81–4). Phalasarna was one of those cities. However, not long thereafter, the Persian Empire collapsed and
   Alexander passed away. These were fortunate circumstances for Phalasarna, since the city was excused from
   her ­commitments to her evanescent sponsor and at the same time avoided possible punishment by Alexander.
   Phalasarna took full advantage of the Persian resources, first by constructing her massive fortifications
on Crete (Sekunda 2004–2009, 597–99; cf. Hadjidaki 2013). Furthermore, Phalasarna expanded her territory
through the colonization of Aigilia. The northern side of the island was selected for the foundation of the
new settlement through targeted movement. From their Cretan metropolis, the Phalasarnians were able to
command an area reaching to the north as far as Antikythera. On the other hand, from their colony at Aigilia,
they could now survey a much more extensive area stretching to the north, as far as Kythera, Laconia and the
Cyclades. Phalasarna may have also used part of the Persian money to expand her fleet. Thus, during the next
two and half centuries, the Phalasarnians exercised a form of state-directed piracy. In that respect, they were not

The 2nd century BCE witnessed the establishment of Rome as a major power in the Mediterranean. In the
course of this century, Rome was gradually involved in disputes among Hellenistic monarchs and Greek states.
Taking advantage of the constant fights among the Greeks, the Romans managed to expand their influence on
the Aegean and finally dominate in the area (Waterfield 2014). At the same time, their increasing acquaintance
with Greek culture led to a growing demand for pieces of Greek art and other refined products (Pollitt 1986,
159–62). This caused the gradual enhancement of the maritime trade between Italy and the Aegean. The de-
vouring demand for Greek products has left its imprint on Cicero’s writings, who was also an eager collector
(CLA 1.8.2, 1.9.2, 1.10.3; cf. Bouyia 2012a 278, 280–82; 2012b). This phenomenon further intensified in the
early 1st century BCE and allegedly spiked immediately after 71 BCE, as a result of the devastating effects of the
Spartacus rebellion; the desire to refurbish wiped private and public buildings in the Italian peninsula may have
stimulated the demand for refined Greek products. Undoubtedly, under such circumstances, pirates who could
access trade routes connecting Italy and the Aegean were presented with golden opportunities.
     Against this background, the discovery of the Antikythera wreck very close to the pirate’s nest of Aigilia
is a striking fact that deserves closer examination. First, the shipwreck was apparently discovered far beyond
­established routes of maritime trade throughout antiquity. This conclusion is supported by the fact that no other
 shipwrecks have been discovered in this area. The presence of pirates on the north side of Antikythera for most
 of the Hellenistic period was not the only factor that discouraged commercial ships from sailing through this
 area. Ancient sailors avoided sailing through the open sea, as they regarded coastal routes as much safer against
 weather’s volatile tempers. The safest and preferable route leading from the Aegean to the Ionian Sea passed
 through the Elaphonissos Strait, between Laconia and the island of Kythera (Fig. 8) (Casson 1991, 142, 179).
 This would also be the expected route for the Antikythera ship, given its arguable itinerary from Delos to Italy
 (Bouyia 2012b, 290–1). The distribution of several shipwrecks along the coasts of Laconia and the eastern coast
 of Kythera allows us to trace this maritime route (Strauss 2024).

acting as a competitor of Metellus. In 67 BCE, the Roman Senate authorized Pompey, under Lex Gabinia, to clean
the Mediterranean from piracy (Tröster 2009). The Roman campaign ended with the subordination of Crete

have much deeper than simply utilitarian motives; both sides may well have perceived it as an act of war. Even
though a route through the Elaphonissos Strait runs far from Antikythera, at the same time it was within the
operational range of the Aigilian pirates. After a sudden attack, the pirates may have captured and subsequently
hauled the vessel to their island. However, the massive size of the ship –its capacity was estimated at approxi-

from leading it into the small harbor of their city. Instead, they anchored the ship next to the little Thymonies
Bay, namely just to the east of the city. Not long afterwards, it ended up on the seabed, while the A

probably negotiating its return to the Romans for ransom.
     With respect to the detailed circumstances of its sinking, we believe that there are several possible
­explanations. Perhaps the pirates themselves sank it on purpose, on the prospect of a Roman attack. On the
 other hand, an outbreak of a strong north wind would have made the overloaded ship extremely vulnerable. It
 is also worth mentioning that if the Antikythera shipwreck was a pirate’s victim, it was probably not unique in
 that respect; the excavators of the Kyrenia shipwreck have also proposed that the sinking of that ship was caused
 by a pirates’ attack (for discussion and bibliography, see Schmitt and Kieburg 2016).

other ancient shipwrecks have been reported in this area. These facts seem even stranger if we take into a­ ccount

striving to clear the Aegean from piracy. This entails that a commercial ship full of precious cargo, serving

The island of Kythera is located upon one of the most dangerous passages, of one of the most important maritime routes of
the Mediterranean. Subsequently, the island’s geostrategic value was exploited for commercial, military and p­ aramilitary
purposes by various agents throughout its known history. Generally accepted as prominent prowling grounds, pirate
­activity in the waters off Kythera is well attested during the early modern times but remains fragmented during antiquity.
 Additionally, the operational specifics determining pirate activity in the region remain unclear.
In order to investigate pirate activity in Kythera across time and delineate the modus operandi of attacks at sea, this study
utilizes a geo-archaeological approach – namely the investigation of the fundamental geomorphological parameters and
technological constraints defining navigation in the region, in order to define specific potent zones of operation off the
island’s coasts, and the subsequent reassessment of associated archaeological remains identified along its coastline.
The present study is the result of a wider, ongoing, geo-archaeological investigation of the island’s maritime history. It
­utilizes textual and iconographical sources, as well as current geomorphological, historical and archaeological r­ esearch.
 This corpus is complemented by historical cartography, cross-examined with present-day data, reports from local m
                                                                                                                 ­ ariners
 recently interviewed and field observations conducted by the author.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The multi-faceted subject of piracy in antiquity has been the focus of significant studies (e.g., Ormerod 1924;
Brulé 1978; Gabbert 1986; de Souza 1999; Gabrielsen 2001, 2003, 2013; Lewis 2019), with some scholars ­focusing
on different aspects (see, for example, de Souza 1999 on a political and historiographic and Gabrielsen 2001,
2003, 2013 on a socio-economic perspective). However, one essential aspect has received much less attention –
namely, “the pragmatic issue of how it played out in practice” (Lewis 2019, 81), especially at sea.
   In order to approach this practical aspect, it is necessary to focus on the fact that piracy is interwoven with
seamanship (e.g., Ormerod 1924, 31). Even in its most simple form, of piracy as “violence at sea”, robbing-at-sea
requires the competence and skills necessary to operate a boat, under challenging conditions. In essence, pirates
and corsairs are armed seamen, and that last feature is a defining parameter that delimits their effectiveness. As
such, to approach this aspect of piracy, it is necessary to address basic parameters of seamanship, such as the
practical limitations imposed by logistics-at-sea, the technological constraints imposed by contemporary naval

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
technology, as well as the contemporary developments in naval warfare, and most importantly, the navigation
specifics imposed by geomorphology at a local scale.
    This investigation focuses on this particular aspect, using the island of Kythera as a case study. Even though
the island rarely appears in sources, its rich history is well-attested in several important archaeological sites
(for an overview on archaeological remains identified in Kythera, see Gregory and Tzortzopoulou-Gregory
2015). What makes the island a particularly interesting case for this study is its location along one of the most
important, lucrative and dangerous marine passages in the Mediterranean.
       In order to investigate pirate activity off the waters of Kythera and its archaeological imprint along the
i­sland’s coast, this study utilizes a geo-archaeological approach. This approach aims to define the fundamental
 ­geomorphological parameters determining navigation in the region and, as a result, the island’s geostra-
  tegic s­ignificance within wider Mediterranean marine networks. Then, an attempt is made to correlate this
  ­geostrategic significance with both attested and inferred pirate and corsair activity throughout its documented
   history, in order to evaluate specific potent zones of operation off the island’s coasts and, subsequently, to
   ­propose a ­reassessment of coastal archaeological remains that can be associated with pirate activity.
    The present study is the result of a wider, ongoing, geo-archaeological investigation of the island’s maritime
history. It utilizes (a) textual, iconographic and cartographic sources dating from antiquity until modern times,
(b) published geomorphological, historical and archaeological research, (c) present-day data such as satellite
imagery, digital elevation models, meteorological reports, sailing guides and nautical charts, (d) reports from
local seamen interviewed between 2022 and 2023, and (e) field observations conducted by the author. The
above have been integrated into a geo-referenced database realized on an open-source Geographic Information
System software (QGiS). It is a fundamental tool of this study, facilitating the investigation of spatial organiza-
tion and relations, extrapolation of information from cartographic sources, cross-referencing with present-day
data, as well as implementing this study’s results into future research.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Piracy
Naturally, whenever naval control of the region would wane, a passage of such prominent commercial activity
would also attract the interest of pirates or, in case of antagonizing naval powers, corsairs. During such periods,
as the following historical review clearly demonstrates, the Kythera channel would constitute ideal hunting
grounds (see also Ormerod 1924, 20–1).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Classical period
The earliest mention attesting to pirate activity in Kythera dates from the Classical period: Thucydides describes
Kythera as “an island lying off Laconia, opposite Maleaσ, the inhabitants are Lacedaemonians of the class of the
Perioeci; and an officer called the Judge of Cythera went over to the place annually from Sparta. A garrison of
heavy infantry was also regularly sent there, and great attention paid to the island, as it was the landing-place
for the merchantmen from Egypt and Libya, and at the same time secured Laconia from the attacks of privateers
from the sea, at the only point where it is assailable, as the whole coast rises abruptly towards the Sicilian and
Cretan seas” (Thuc. 4.53.2–3, trans. J.M. Dent, London and New York, 1910). The passage provides a rich con-
text regarding the complex relationship between maritime commerce and piracy control in the region during
the time: Thucydides identifies the island as a station of a trading route reaching from the north African coast
to the Greek mainland; signifies both the value and the threat that the island’s location posed for the Laconian
coast; and specifies how privateers operated in the area.
     In contrast to the Classical period, assessing pirate activity in Kythera in later period is challenging, as
the ­island appears only sporadically in textual sources until the early modern times. However, quite some
­information can be extrapolated from relevant mentions.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Hellenistic period
The eastern Mediterranean saw a significant rise of piracy and privateering during the Hellenistic period
(Ormerod 1924, 114–50; Gabbert 1986; de Souza 1999, 43–96; Gabrielsen 2001; 2003; 2013, 143–51). Cretans
are repeatedly presented in sources of the period as engaging in piracy and privateering (e.g., Diod. Sic. 27.3.1,
40.1.3; Plut. Pomp. 29.1; Polyb. 4.8.12, 13.8.1; Strab. 10.4.9–10), operating in the Aegean (Ormerod 1924, 131,
144–48; Brulé 1978, 2–115; de Souza 1999, 80–4) – as well as slave markets flourishing in certain Cretan cities,
including Polyrrhenia at the tip of western Crete (de Souza 1999, 57–63; for a summary of the historical and ar-
chaeological data for Polyrrhenia see Perlman 2004, 1182–83). At the same time, from the Ionian Sea and along
the south coast of the Peloponnese, relevant mentions include an attack by Illyrians on the Messenian coast
in 230 BCE commented as being “from time immemorial the scene of the raids of the Illyrians” (Polyb. 2.5.1,
trans. E.S. Shuckburgh, London and New York, 1889), an episode describing the capture of people from ancient

Mothone (Paus. 4.35.6–7) and a mention about a fleet of 15 galleys plundering and capturing the merchants
between ­Lefkada and Cape Maleas in 217 BCE (Polyb. 5.95.1–4). With pirates and privateers operating on both
sides of and along the south Peloponnese passage, it stands to reason that the Kythera straits would constitute
a hotspot at the time.
    Textual evidence suggests that this was indeed the case at least during the late 3rd–early 2nd century BCE.
In 221/220 BC, privateers captured a royal vessel of Macedonia, near Kythera: “By sea they immediately sent out
privateers, who, falling in with a royal vessel of Macedonia near Cythera, brought it with all its crew to A
                                                                                                           ­ itolia,
and sold ship-owners, sailors, and marines, and finally the ship itself ” (Polyb. 4.6.1, trans. E.S. Shuckburgh,
London and New York, 1889). Presumably, during the reign of Nabis, tyrant of Sparta (207–192 BCE), and in
consort with Cretan pirates, Sparta was used as a base of operations: “He [Nabis] made common cause with the
Cretan pirates, and kept temple-breakers, highway-robbers, and murderers all over the Peloponnese; and as he
shared in the profits of their nefarious trades, he allowed them to use Sparta as their base of operations” (Polyb.
13.8.1, trans. E.S. Shuckburgh, London and New York, 1889). Reportedly, Nabis “made the waters off Maleum
a dangerous area [for the Romans] with his pirate vessels”, targeting “ships transporting supplies”, and “had the
entire coastline from Cape Malea at the mercy of his pirate vessels” (Livy 34.32.12, 34.36.3, trans. J.C. Yardley,
Cambridge, Mass., 2017). Even though the island is not directly mentioned, the Maleas-Kythera passage would
most probably constitute the main zone of pirate operations.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Roman period
Both the three-year long campaign of Metellus against Crete, which started in 69 BCE and culminated in the
conquest of the island (Diod. Sic. 40.1.1–3; App. Sic. 6.1–2; de Souza 1999, 158–61), as well as the campaign of
Pompey against pirates in 67 BCΕ (Plut. Pomp. 26.3–4; Ormerod 1924, 234–41; de Souza 1999, 167–78), surely
halted pirate operations in the strait: not only was Crete and its harbors brought under Roman control, but also
a naval fleet operated between Delos and Sicily (Varro, Rust. 2, Introduction 6.2). However, Pompey’s campaign
was only temporarily effective (de Souza 1999, 179–85). In the second half of the 1st century BCE, during the
Roman civil wars, piracy once again became a serious threat in the Mediterranean (Ormerod 1924, 248–56; de
Souza 1999, 185–95). At the time, “the sea was left unguarded” and Cilician pirates are reported as operating
also at Cape Tainaron (Matapan), right across Kythera (Plut. Pomp. 24.2–5, trans. B. Perrin, Cambridge, Mass.,
1917).
    Roman control at the passage was most probably restored after the naval battle at Actium (31 BCE). ­Augustus,
in order to reward the Spartans for their aid at Actium, presented Kythera to C. Julius Eurycles of Sparta (Strabo
8.5.1; Cass. Dio 54.7.2). Interestingly enough, his father Lachares had been executed, apparently on the charge
of piracy (Plut. Ant. 67.2–3; for Eurycles and the dynasty of the Euryclids see Bowersock 1961; Steinhaouer
2006–2007, 2010). In the following centuries and for the first time in its known history, the Mediterranean is
under the control of a single political unit and piracy is systematically suppressed along its coastline – even if the
phenomenon does not completely disappear (de Souza 1999, 196–210). But perhaps relatedly, so does Kythera
from surviving sources.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Modus operandi of attacks at sea
Investigating the practical aspects of piracy, especially during antiquity, is inherently difficult. Αn attack at sea
is usually a brief and violent event happening far from uninvolved witnesses. Pirates themselves are unlikely
sources of information. Their surviving victims are more probable sources, but even in such cases, the details of
major events, such as raids on coastal settlements, are much more likely to survive through history (Lewis 2019,
89) rather than accounts of individual cases of attacks at sea.
     Such events hardly leave any clearly discernible archaeological traces. Even though agile oared galleys
would be the preferred craft of choice (Casson 1971, 125–32; Krantonelli 1985, 337–56; 1998, 285–303), there
is no type of vessel that was exclusively used for piracy (see, for example, Gabrielsen 2001, 223–28; Nakas, this
volume). Furthermore, defining the circumstances behind a wreck event is extremely difficult and there is no
telltale evidence that can be directly associated with an attack at sea with certainty, not to mention the further
attribution of roles such as “pirate” or “victim”.
