findings.evidence_excerpt:
In the case of Kythera, given the scarce information provided by ancient sources, studying pirate operations
at the passage during antiquity is by default severely limited. On the other hand, the numerous reports of attacks
on the island’s waters dating from early modern times can provide a valuable frame of reference. Most attacks,
however, are simply described as happening “off Kythera” (e.g., Krantonelli 1985, 52, 57–8, 163–64; 1991, 47,
71, 115, 163–64; 1998, 25, 28, 45, 89–91, 130, 158, 236). Even when reports include more details, their interest
usually lies at documenting damage and losses, rather than providing specifics on the event itself. As such, there
is very few information on fundamental operational specifics, such as where, how and under which conditions
did pirate ships attack their prey on the passage – necessary information that can assist in investigating pirate
operations also during antiquity. Given the limited underwater research conducted along the island’s littoral,
attempting to assess the specifics of pirate and corsair activity in Kythera through archaeological proxies is
challenging.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Local navigation conditions
To investigate the way in which pirates operated on the passage during antiquity, certain elements can be
­extrapolated by examining the fundamental environmental parameters defining navigation in the area, such as
 the island’s geomorphology and prevailing winds, and contemporary naval technology constraints. Combined
 with the strategies that are known to have been commonly used by pirates in the area, the above can be used to
 delineate specifics of pirate activity on the waters of Kythera diachronically.
     In general, pirates would prefer to target easy prey, such as ships struggling on difficult navigation ­conditions.
Bold and experienced sailors, they would know the waters where they operated much better than passing
­merchants (Ormerod 1924, 31). Also, as mentioned above, they had the significant advantage of using agile
 rowed galleys, able to maneuver much better than bulky sailing ships. As such, instead of attacks at the open
 sea under good conditions, were they could not employ those advantages, they would target either on becalmed
 vessels (Ormerod 1924, 16; Lewis 2019, 90–1) or on vessels struggling under difficult sailing conditions – such
 as on dangerous coasts and narrows (Krantonelli 1985, 357–58), where sailing ships would be forced to turning
 in order to avoid collisions, while at the same time catching the wind (G. Trikaliotis, pers. comm.).
    In view of this, both the narrow passage between Kythera and Maleas, as well as the island’s rocky and often
inaccessible coastline, whose few potent harbor locations dictate predictable choice of shelter, constitute ideal
hunting grounds. Entering the Kythera-Maleas passage from the north is a sharp turn for large sailing ships.
Under strong prevailing (north/northeastern) winds, they are forced into a series of turns, towards the north-
eastern coast of Kythera, with a turning point a few kilometers off Ayia Pelagia, before being able to turn again
into the channel (Fig. 2). Not a dangerous point but a demanding one for large sailing ships, it constitutes a
probable and most of all predictable attack location. Stronger north/northeastern winds force sailing vessels
even further south, where their best option is to shelter at the cove of Ayios Nikolaos. Likewise, sailing into the
passage from the west under similar conditions forces ships to seek shelter at Routsounas or further south to
Ocheles. Lastly, strong western winds force large sailing ships towards specific protected anchorages at the east
or the south coast, namely Ayia Pelagia, Ayios Nikolaos, Kapsali and Melidoni (G. Trikaliotis, pers. comm.).
Given the predictability of those scenarios, pirates would specifically target the passages towards those safe
havens, depending on prevailing wind conditions (e.g., de Nicolay 1577, 56–58).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Potent ambush points
As for where pirate ships could be stationed, a highly probably choice would be the practice of using hidden
coves and headlands as ambush points (Ormerod 1924, 17–25). Their vessels concealed, by keeping watch for
victims from nearby elevated positions, pirates would pounce at unsuspecting victims – a method well-attested
in the Aegean (e.g., Hacke 1699, 8; Krantonelli 1985, 358) and in Kythera specifically (Krantonelli 1998, 150)
during the early modern times. Similar tactics were used in antiquity (Lewis 2019, 90–2) and are attested a­ lready

findings.evidence_excerpt:
in the Odyssey: the suitors waited to ambush Telemachus by a rocky islet with “a harbor where ships may lie,
with an entrance on either side”, while “day by day watchmen sat upon the windy heights” (Od. 4.846–847 and
16.365–366, respectively, trans. A.T. Murray, Cambridge, Mass., 1919). Likewise, centuries later, Heliodorus
describes pirates waiting in ambush hidden by a promontory (Aeth. 5.20).
    On the other hand, it should be stressed that not every cove and islet would serve as “a lurking-ground to
catch merchantmen” (Ormerod 1924, 22). In practice, there are necessary conditions that would constitute an
ambush point effective:
   (a) a potent natural harbor or anchorage, easily accessible, providing sufficient shelter from prevailing winds
and swells, as well as safe anchoring or beaching conditions (of a suitable depth and seabed type),
    (b) located upon marine routes, but at the same time at a safe distance from policing forces,
    (c) providing visual cover from passing ships, while offering vantage points on incoming traffic, and
    (d) access to freshwater resources.
   In this regard, the only locations meeting those conditions in Kythera are the coves of Routsounas, Vani,
Melidoni and Vroulea (Fig. 4):
    Routsounas is a small natural harbor at a most advantageous location by the northwestern tip of Kythera.
It provides good anchoring conditions and shelter from northern and northeastern prevailing winds. The bay
provides visual cover to a few vessels anchored within, and the surrounding hills offer vantage points. Until
recently, freshwater could be easily acquired from a coastal spring throughout the year (G. Trikaliotis, pers.
comm.). The cove appears on 16th-century nautical charts, such as those of Gaspar Luis Viegas and Antonio
Millo (2006). Conveniently located upon the Peloponnese-Kythera strait, safe from prevailing winds and with

both on the passages along the west coast of Kythera, as well as upon the bustling northern passage along the
Peloponnese coast (for more on Routsounas see also Markakis forthcoming).
    The cove of Melidoni is a potent natural harbor by the southwest tip of the island. The roadstead provides
shelter from all prevailing winds, good anchoring conditions and can accommodate even a few large vessels (G.
Trikaliotis, pers. comm.). The bay provides excellent cover to vessels within, and easy access to the surrounding
hills. Similar conditions are provided at the nearby cove of Vani, only 2 km to the northwest. Both coves also
appear noted on the aforementioned 16th-century nautical charts. Freshwater could perhaps be acquired at the
nearby small bay at Feloti, 1.5 km to the east (Danamos 1992, 312; Aggelidis et al. 2016, 16). As such, both coves
constitute ideal ambush points against vessels sailing along the west and south coasts of Kythera. It should also
be noted that mentions in sources from the 18th century suggest a connection with Cretan corsairs based in
Kythera, possibly operating from Melidoni (Krantonelli 1998, 98–101).
    Vroulea, a small cove at the southeast tip of the island provides sufficient shelter from prevailing winds (even
though it is affected by northeastern winds), good anchoring (G. Trikaliotis, pers. comm.) and possibly access
to freshwater (Danamos 1992, 312; Aggelidis et al. 2016, 19). It can accommodate only a few but well-hidden
vessels and the surrounding hills provide for vantage points. Therefore, the cove is a potent ambush point at a
critical location, against vessels passing along the south and east coasts of Kythera.
    Closing this section, it is important to note that –except for Melidoni under certain conditions– none of
the above locations could function as a permanent base of operations. As with every natural harbor location
in present-day Kythera, none of those coves provide all-weather shelter. As such, unless beached, pirate vessels
would have to relocate quite often.

At the southern islet, Dragonera, pottery fragments attest to human presence since the Early Helladic period.
Ceramic scatters dating mainly from the Hellenistic period have been identified on the eastern low hill, while
on the western hill stand the remains of a structure at least 25x30 m. in size, with a sizable built cistern in its
center. Outside it, more structures and cisterns have been found. It has been interpreted as a fort, possibly dating
after the 6th–7th centuries (Gregory and Tzortzopoulou-Gregory 2015, 128–30), reflecting an attempt of the
Byzantine empire, threatened by the Arab expansion and the ensuing rise of piracy in the coastline of Greece
and the Aegean (de Souza 1999, 238–39), to retain control of the seaways towards the western Mediterranean by
establishing minor control points even on small coves and islets (Poulou-Papadimitriou 2013, 172–75).

vantageous location providing reach against vessels sailing both alongside the east coast of Kythera, on the
route ­connecting Crete and the north African coast with the Greek mainland and beyond, and towards Ayios

16th and early 19th century (de Nicolay 1557, 61; Saint-Sauveur 1800, 331; see also Krantonelli 1991, 197; 1998,
240). Based on these mentions and the location’s capacity, it stands to reason that it would have been used as
such by their predecessors as well. In this context, the remains identified at Antidragonera can be seen under a
completely different perspective: as the remains of a loot cache. Under such a light, many previously puzzling
elements can be reasoned with, such as:
    (a) The site’s limited accessibility and isolation – which would constitute an advantage.
    (b) The amount and heterogeneity of the reported remains, the majority of which can be divided in three
types: (1) personal items of value, such as seal stones of semi-precious materials and coins, (2) common m­ aritime
trade cargo, such as amphorae and fine-ware, (3) probably construction material, such as tiles and nails. The
reason behind the occurrence of the first two types on a loot cache is self-evident, but the third less so. Even
though tiles are attested as maritime trade cargo material (Rico 1995; Carre 2021), presently, there is not enough
information to support such a notion. In theory, a provisional wooden structure such as the one proposed by
the excavators (Tsaravopoulos and Fragou 2017, 130; 2020, 322) could also correspond to one used by pirates –
perhaps a hideout or a signal station, as mentioned in a text from the 1st century BCE (Plut. Pomp. 24.3).
    (c) Both the high number and the wide spatial distribution of the identified coins, reflecting a sample of
the total inter-Mediterranean maritime traffic passing through the Peloponnese-Crete strait, rather than only
sailors under specific conditions.
    (d) The chronological frame of use of the site as provided by those coins, which not only corresponds to a
­period of increased pirate activity in the region, but it also terminates with the establishment of Roman ­influence
and the subsequent imposition of order at sea – the latter providing for a reason behind the site’s discontinued
use.

can only be investigated by further, detailed analysis of the remains themselves, whose number is described as

findings.evidence_excerpt:
The Kythera-Maleas passage constitutes a key location for marine traffic since antiquity. Upon significant
­maritime crossroads, the island served as a major traffic enabler, providing shelter at one of the most important
 and most dangerous passages of the Mediterranean. At the same time, the island’s waters provided the ideal
 setting for pirate operations: difficult navigation conditions, potent ambush locations and supply availability
 made for ideal hunting grounds, upon a most lucrative zone. Evidence clearly suggests increased pirate ac-
 tivity in Kythera in periods of crisis, whenever naval control at the passage would weaken – such as during
 the ­Hellenistic period, the 6th–8th centuries, the period of the Venetian-Ottoman wars and the collapse of the
 Republic of Venice.
    By investigating fundamental navigation parameters, surviving mentions in written sources and reported
incidents, significant information regarding operational specifics off the Kytherian coasts can be extrapolated.
The most potent attack zone seems to be the northeast/east coast (Ayia Pelagia and Ayios Nikolaos). Moreover,
the most likely locations for pirate ships to be stationed in ambush are the coves by the northwest, southwest
and southeast tips of the island (Routsounas, Vani, Melidoni, Vroulea).
    Finally, for the study of piracy in the wider Kythera region, the Dragoneres presents great interest. Based
on the area’s geomorphology and its attested use in later periods, it is proposed that the location served as an
ambush point frequented by pirates also during antiquity. This interpretation can be correlated with the site at
Antidragonera, which in this study is suggested to have been a loot cache, and possibly with finds and structural
remains at Dragonera, and naval remains in the surrounding waters. In general, the sites at Dragonera provide
a very rich archaeological archive for unknown periods of Kythera’s history and further meticulous research
could shed more light on the most intriguing topics of maritime sanctuaries, pirate activity and naval warfare in
antiquity. As for the site at Antidragonera, whether those valuables were deposited by their rightful owners or
extracted by pirates, the most significant element remains: they attest to the strategic importance of Kythera as a
key location for ­maritime traffic spanning the entire Mediterranean, for both sailors, traders, navies and pirates.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Despite the numerous references in ancient written sources to pirate practices, actions and persons, identifying
­archaeological evidence linked to piracy is undoubtedly very difficult. This difficulty can possibly be overcome by the
 systematic investigation of the numerous islets in the Greek seas. As the relevant sources testify, these islets, which did not
 constitute a fertile ground for normal living or cultural development, being far from the sight of the rest of society and
 close to sea routes, were ideal pirate places throughout time.
This paper discusses first the various uses of the islets by pirates −a long-standing pirate practice, as revealed by the written
sources− and some methodological considerations that emerged during the A.P.Pir.A. project, which can c­ ontribute to the
identification of archaeological sites as possible pirate bases. Then, it examines the site of Kastraki on Agathonisi in the
northern Dodecanese, between Samos and Miletus, which is an excellent case study, as it is one of the few ­systematically
excavated and published sites on a Greek islet. After a brief consideration of the pirate activity in the wider area of Samos
and Miletus, a review of the archaeological findings is attempted in the light of the archaeology of piracy. Thus, in
­addition to the existing interpretations on the fort’s various uses, the present paper proposes another possible function of
 this site, that of a pirate base.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Pirate activity in the Greek seas seems to have been a constant phenomenon in antiquity. It is indicative that in
the database of the A.P.Pir.A. project, the number of entries with references to piracy in the Greek seas during
antiquity is close to 500 (see more in Samaras, this volume). These references, of course, concern only incidents,
places and persons that happened to be recorded in a written source; in real terms, the incidents, places and
persons related to piracy in antiquity were probably limitless. On the other hand, the number of examples that
can be demonstrated archaeologically is, so far, quite limited.
      The study of references to piracy in ancient literature provides a useful contribution to this issue, as it
­reveals the frequency and modes of operation that ancient pirates employed. For example, it is significant that,
 ­according to Aristotle (Pol. 1256a–b), brigandage is listed among the five primary ways of human subsistence,
  alongside pastoralism, fishing, agriculture and hunting. Indeed, he points out that some of these occupations
  are occasionally combined to offset the limitations of a single occupation, and cites as an example the fact that

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
some peoples combine the practice of pastoralism with that of banditry. This reference illuminates the character
of piracy in antiquity, which was an occupation less reprehensible historically than it is considered today. In past
eras piracy was very common and almost always in occurrence. It should certainly be noted that the frequency
and intensity of pirate activity experienced fluctuations throughout antiquity, which were of course directly re-
lated to corresponding social, political and economic circumstances. However, the study of the history of piracy
by the A.P.Pir.A. project has highlighted certain diachronic characteristics of this phenomenon, including the
variation in public perceptions of piracy on one’s relationship to its practice (perpetrator or victim) (Samaras,
this volume).
    Initially, as Thucydides mentions (1.8.1), the peoples of the coastal areas, especially islanders, were the ones
who most commonly indulged in piracy. Plutarch’s (Cim. 8.3) reference to piracy by the Skyrians is emblematic,
since they did not exploit their land well, turned to maritime activities and resorted to piracy, often robbing the
very merchants with whom they cooperated. Allowing for the perception that pirate behavior was viewed not
only as something not reprehensible but also as a show of bravery (Thuc. 1.5.1), the likelihood arises that every
islander was a potential pirate when circumstances warranted. Indeed, even members of the social elite might
engage in piracy, such as the tyrant of Samos, Polycrates, who seems to have carried out systematic piracy (Hdt.
3.39.3−4; for Polycrates’ possible pirate activity see Carty 2015, esp. 144−48; Kuciak 2020; contra Jackson 2000,
143). Besides Polycrates, there are many examples of piracy conducted by rulers (see for example Dem. 4.34
and 50.4 on Philip II and Alexander of Pherai, respectively), or even by large cities (e.g., Thuc. 6.4.5 [Zancle],
7.26.1−3 [Athens]; Paus. 4.23.7 [Zancle]; Diod. Sic. 27.1.1 [Sparta]; Hadjidaki 1988, 476 [Phalasarna]). On the
other hand, as is widely known, ancient naval powers frequently advertised the containment or even the effec-
tive suppression of piracy, actions that in fact seem to have been carried out with limited success (Engels 2016,
292−308). However, it is important to note that the official authorities did not exclusively pursue pirates, but
often collaborated with them (see indicatively on Demetrius I Poliorcetes: Diod. Sic. 20.82.4, and on Mithri-
dates: App. Mith. 9.63. Also, de Souza 1999, 116−18; Gabrielsen 2013, 146, 150).
    Pirates were most often citizens of “normal” cities, living together with the “normal” members of society.
However, when they turned to piracy for whatever reason, they usually needed places far away from their
homeland and far from the eyes of respectable society, either for the purposes of preparation for piracy, for the
act of piracy itself, or for the management of booty, captives and ransom payments in the wake of a successful
piratical action. Another reason for the need to select remote places, from which to operate and, by extension,
conceal one’s identity, was the fact that the victims of piracy would often attack the pirates’ homelands in re-
prisal ­(Gabrielsen 2013, 143−45). For these and other reasons mentioned below, the small uninhabited islands
and ­islets (i.e., small islands up to 15 km2 as they are defined in this paper) of the Greek seas represented an
important station in the almost indiscriminate exercise of piracy.
    Since islets were used quite often by pirates, the question arises whether it is possible to identify the remains
of piracy archaeologically at these locations. Unfortunately, very few islets have been the subject to systematic
archaeological investigation in this regard.1 Utilizing the methodological approach of the archaeology of piracy
developed by the A.P.Pir.A. project, this paper attempts to answer this question by choosing Agathonisi, an islet
in the northern Dodecanese, between Samos and Miletus, as a case study. The location is presented for two main
reasons. First, the excavation at the site of Kastraki by the Ephorate of Antiquities of the Dodecanese, under
the direction of Dr. Pavlos Triantafyllidis, and the publication of its findings presents Agathonisi as an excellent
case study of a systematic archaeological investigation of an islet. Secondly, the site dates to a period (1st century
BCE) and a region (Aegean), where written sources attest that piracy was on the increase (e.g., Diod. Sic. 27.3.1;
Cic. Leg. Man. 35; Plut. Pomp. 24.1–25.1; Polyaenus Strat. 5.19.1; see more in de Souza 1999, 43−96; Gabrielsen
2001; Mendoni 2009; Pacheco 2020). Thus, by reviewing the ancient written sources and the archaeological
findings from Kastraki, the possibility that the site functioned at least periodically as a pirate base presents itself.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
It is a known fact that the numerous uninhabited and often arid islets of the Greek seas were fertile ground for
the practice of piracy throughout history. Any sailor, who wanted to attempt piracy, could conquer or tempo-
rarily reside on an islet unhindered. The various needs of the pirates could be easily satisfied on such remote
locations, including bases from which to lurk and ambush, as well as stations for the distribution of booty, the
holding of captives while awaiting ransom payments, the concealment of booty, the evasion of identification,
and in general the temporary need to avoid the eyes of the rest of the world.
    A typical example of pirate exploitation of small islands is described in two passages of Demosthenes
(7.3; 12.12−13) concerning the Peparethian pirate Sostratos and his base on Halonnesos − identified by most
scholars as the remote small island Ayios Efstratios (Reger 2004, 733; for all islands and islets mentioned in this
section, see Fig. 1). According to Demosthenes, all pirates conquer foreign lands, fortify them and from these
strongholds launch raids against others (for a broader discussion of the use of small islands as raiding bases see
Constantakopoulou 2007, 115–19). This pirate tactic is likewise stressed by Thucydides (4.53.3), who mentions
that the Spartans were worried that their opponents would capture Kythera, using it as a stronghold from which
to conduct pirate raids in Laconia. The islet of Myonessos in the straits of Artemision likewise ­appears to have
served as a potential pirate base (Aeschin. Leg. 72; Strabo 9.5.14).
    The usefulness of islets as hiding places for ambushing emerges from the description of Polyxenidas’ tactic,
who at the beginning of the 2nd century BCE, was hiding with his few ships behind the Cape Myonessos and
the islets of Makris and Aethalia, while awaiting the best opportunity to surprise a passing Roman fleet (Liv.
37.12.1−3). The Myonessos mentioned here is not the aforementioned islet in the Strait of Artemision, but rather
a cape-islet at Ionia that was also used by pirates. Livy (37.27.4−8) records that the Roman fleet, while passing
from Samos to Chios, observed some pirate ships returning from a raid on Chios. The Roman fleet rushed to

expel the pirates, with the latter taking refuge in a naturally protected cape-islet, called Myonessos, ­resulting in
a time-consuming and ultimately unsuccessful assault by the Romans, who were unable to o      ­ vercome the natural
advantages of the site.
   One of the most typical examples of an islet as a pirate site arises from an inscription found at Syros (IG XII.5
653), which narrates an interesting account of piracy (de Souza 1999, 185; Nocita and Guizzi 2005; Mendoni
2009): after a raid on the country and city of Syros, a band of pirates headed with their captives to the ­imminent
opposite island of the chora of Siphnians, which is identified by most scholars as Kitriani (Reger 1994, 262;
Nocita and Guizzi 2005, 281; Pantou and Papadopoulou 2005, 92−3; Constantakopoulou 2007, 196). This islet
provided the pirates either with a useful location for ransom exchanges, or with a hideout and den for raids.
    Something similar happened at the islet of Pharmakoussa, where pirates, who captured young Julius Caesar
as a hostage, reportedly took refuge (see below). The “commercial” phase of the piratical process began with
the determination of the ransom payment and required that they remained at Pharmakoussa, while waiting for
Julius Caesar’s supporters to assemble it. In this instance, it becomes clear that the pirates were little more than
armed merchants, who immediately after conducting the raid, pursued negotiations for the ransom. For this
reason, it was convenient for them to remain temporarily on a deserted island at a short distance from the place
they had plundered, to await the ransom payment before relocating to a more advantageous harbor (Gabrielsen
2013, 148−52).
    Numerous similar cases of pirates using Greek islets are also known from later periods, some of which are
presented below as representative cases. For instance, a fortified pirate base of the 5th century CE is mentioned
on the islet of Velopoula in the Myrtoan Sea, between Spetses and Melos (Kyrou 2021, 235). During the 1760s,
the Slavonian pirate Markos Lukovic, in collaboration with English and Greek pirates, operated from the islet of
Proti, close to the west coast of Messenia (Krantonelli 1998, 44−5). More recently, during the early 19th century,
the pirate Nikolaos Katramados (or Giannouzas) from Spetses used Diavolonisia in the Northern Sporades as
his base (Krantonelli 1998, 254).
    All these examples confirm the value of the islets as pirate sites. The use of small islands by pirates −a
­ iachronic choice, as the history of piracy both in ancient and in later times demonstrates− either for p
d                                                                                                        ­ ermanent
settlement or for occasional use, makes them ideal candidates for the archaeological investigation of pirate bases
or stations. Apart from the fact that they were frequently utilized by pirates, Greek islets offer an additional
advantage for the archaeology of piracy. Due to the generally limited extent of their occupation (as opposed
to those of permanent settlements), archaeological remains encountered on uninhabited islets enjoy a higher
likelihood of association with piratical use. For example, some sort of connection with piracy has been sug-
gested for sites on islets, such as the Late Helladic IIIC settlement at Modi (an islet in the Saronic Gulf, at a
short ­distance from Poros) and the fortified Middle Geometric settlement at Vathy Limenari on Donousa in the
Cyclades (Samaras 2015, 196, 199).

In the context of pirate actions and choices, several constant features seem indicative of the character and needs
of pirate activity. The attempt to identify these in archaeological contexts by the A.P.Pir.A. project has resulted
in an established set of criteria that indicate possible pirate activity. The archaeological evidence of piracy may
be reflected both in permanent features and mobile objects, for example in iconography, in votives, in burial
and shipwreck contexts, in remains of destruction caused by pirate raids, in evidence of protection measures
taken against pirate threats, etc. (see also Samaras, this volume). For the identification and correlation of such
contexts with piracy, corresponding criteria have been defined, based on which respective possible archaeo-
logical ­examples have been identified as well. It is a fact that both ancient authors and modern scholars tend
to approach ancient piracy mainly from the victims’ perspective, rather than from that of the perpetrators’

themselves. For example, defensive structures, such as fortifications and towers, are very often considered to
be efforts at anti-piracy protection, while a site is rarely interpreted as a pirate base. For this reason, this paper
focuses on the archaeological evidence of the pirate base.
     The term pirate base is used here to describe any settlement, in which a small or large part of the ­community
is occasionally or consistently occupied with piracy. The size of pirate bases can vary from extremely small
sites to very large settlements. Otherwise, they do not differ substantially from non-pirate settlements, making
them very difficult to distinguish. Nevertheless, pirate bases tend to present certain features, which may help
to ­recognize them. These features constitute potential criteria for identifying pirate bases, as outlined by the
A.P.Pir.A. project (see Samaras, this volume), and are briefly summarized here:
    •     First of all, the choice of location tends to be close to the sea but “invisible”, close to major sea routes,
          yet, seemingly unsuitable for habitation, yet, exhibiting topographical features that are favorable to
          harborage and piratical activities.
    •     In addition, the sites are defensible, whether through selection of naturally defensible sites or through
          the construction of fortifications.
    •     The site displays evidence for occupation of relatively short duration (especially in the case of small
          ­settlements), in combination with the discovery of valuable finds that seem unusual for such a context.
    •     The site exhibits a decidedly maritime orientation with archaeological data indicating that a significant
          part of the community's activities was connected to the sea.
    •     The site exhibits evidence of warlike character, with archaeological data indicating that at least some
          ­members of the community were involved in warlike activities.
    •     The existence of subsequent pirate bases at the same location or in the immediate vicinity, indicating
          that certain topographical features may have favored pirate activity diachronically.
    •     The contextualization of these archaeological sites within a recorded chronological moment in which
          ­piracy is known to have flourished.
     More “specific” criteria could also be added to the above. For example, in the case of piracy during the
­Hellenistic period −on which the present paper focuses− the abandonment of a settlement, the cessation of
 some phase of occupation, or the change of its functions in the period around 67 BCE, when Pompey’s famous
 “anti-pirate” campaign was conducted (de Souza 1999, 149−79), may serve as additional criteria for identifying
 a pirate base.

Pirate activity in the sea area of Samos and Miletus
The islet of Agathonisi is located in the seascape of Samos and Miletus, for which there are several references to
pirate activity in both ancient and modern times (Fig. 2). Starting in the Archaic period, the case of Polycrates,
the tyrant of Samos, has already been mentioned. It is equally possible that Aeaces, Polycrates’s father, also
engaged in piracy (Carty 2015, esp. 53−66; Kuciak 2020, 59; contra Jackson 2000, 144−47). Moreover, several
traditions associate Archaic Samos with piracy, such as an oracle mentioned by Plutarch (Quaest. Graec. 55),
according to which the Samians were told to relocate to the opposite coast of Mycale and to engage in piracy
for a period of ten years in order to defeat their enemies (Thomas 2019, 308−11). An additional oracle related

and Plunkett 1985, no. 647). From this inscription, it is deduced that some unnamed persons asked the oracle
whether it would be justified to commit a raid and Apollo responded affirmatively (Jackson 1995).
     At the beginning of the 5th century BCE, the tyrant of Miletus, Histiaeus, seems to have participated in
­pirate activities (Hdt. 6.5.3, 6.26.1; Blamire 1959, 149−50; Chapman 1972, 566−67), while at the end of the same

 Theopompos, as his messenger (Xen. Hell. 2.1.30; de Souza 1999, 33). In 430/429 BCE, at the beginning of the
 Peloponnesian War, an Athenian flotilla led by Melesander was sent to the region of Caria and Lycia to pre-

 ­merchant ships (Thuc. 2.69.1; Hornblower 1991, 354−56; de Souza 1999, 31−2).
     During the Hellenistic period, a 3rd century BCE inscription from Miletus refers to a treaty between Knossos
and Milesians, according to which the sale of Milesian slaves to Knossos and vice versa was forbidden (IC I viii
6*; for other decrees between Miletus and several Cretan cities, see Carless Unwin 2017, 152). Testimony of this
sort is usually taken as indirect evidence of piracy, as capture by piracy was one of the main sources of slaves.
­Indeed, several such treaties between cities known to have engaged in piracy are on record (de Souza 1999,
 62−3, 68−72; Gabrielsen 2001, 234−36). Even more important for the purposes of this paper is Strabo’s assertion
 that “the island Lade lies close in front of Miletus, as do also the isles in the neighborhood of the Tragaeae, which
 afford anchorage for pirates” (14.1.7, trans. H.L. Jones, Cambridge, Mass., 1929).
    At this point, the case of Julius Caesar’s abduction by pirates outside Pharmakoussa in 75/74 BCE should be
revisited (Ward 1975, 1977; de Souza 1999, 140–41; Osgood 2010, 334–36; Álvarez Pérez-Sostoa 2011, 77–8).
This is undoubtedly the most famous incident of ancient piracy, a fact revealed by its mention by several au-

8.23.1; Suet. Iul. 1−2; De vir. ill. 78.3; Peter, HRRel., Vol. 2, 87 fr. 30; see extensively Günther 1999). Most of

according to whom the pirates captured their famous victim close to Cape Maleas in the Peloponnese and
­remained outside the walls of Miletus until the ransom was delivered. This reference implicitly suggests that
 Pharmakoussa ­belonged to the chora of Miletus.
     Plutarch and Polyaenus refer to the pirates who captured Julius Caesar as Cilicians, while the other sources
 do not specify their identity. Therefore, it cannot be certain whether the pirates were Cilicians, Milesians or
 whether a mixed band − a fairly common occurrence in pirate crews. Perhaps, there was confusion between
 the terms Cilicians and pirates (App. Mith. 14.92) or perhaps the pirates presented themselves as coming from
a distant homeland (e.g., Cilicia), to hide their real identity and to protect (nearby) homeland from repri-
sals, or perhaps the relevant sources, which are all considerably later than the event, wanted to attribute the
incident to some unknown or foreign pirates. Indeed, after the final defeat of Mithridates and the end of the
­Mithridatic wars, cities like Miletus ceased trying to strike a balance between the two conflicting powers (Rome
 and ­Mithridates) and sided, willingly or unwillingly, with Rome (see Kleiner 1968, 19; Sarantidis 2020, 55−6;
 Cicero (Verr. 2.1.89), likewise, refers to the imposition of taxes “by the Roman people” and the participation of
 Miletus in the expulsion of the pirates).
   In any event, whether the pirates had Pharmakoussa as their base or were operating outside of it, or
whether they happened to locate themselves in the vicinity only once, it is difficult to accept the idea that they
went ­unnoticed by a passing ship or by guard troops, given the presence of defensive forts and watchtowers
throughout the Milesian seaboard territories, including those on Pharmakoussa itself (for the supervision of
these islands, see Sarantidis 2020, 203–23, figs. 112–21). Moreover, both the undisturbed visit of a large group of
men anchored in an island cove for thirty-eight days, and the fact that Julius Caesar himself, after he redeemed
himself and assembled a fleet, returned to the island to find the pirates still situated at the same place, would
seem to indicate that the pirates in question were able to reside on these islands (or, at least, on Pharmakoussa)
and conduct their activities unhindered during this period.
    However, pirate activity in this islandscape was not limited to antiquity; in fact, pirates continued to operate
there in modern times. The Englishman Anthony Roberts, a pirate who was himself taken hostage by pirates in
1692, describes the seasonal but systematic use of the region by pirates, stating that after wintering on islands,
such as Paros, Antiparos, Ios and Melos, pirates would sail to Phournoi in early March: “And then they go for the
Furnoes [Phournoi], and lie there under the high land hid, having a watch on the hill with a little flag, whereby
they make a signal, if they see any sail; they flip out, and lie athwart the boak of Samos, and take their prize;
they lie in the same nature under Necaria [Ikaria], and Gadronise [Gaidouronisi], and Leppiso [Leipsoi] in
the spring and forepart of the summer” (Hacke 1699, 8; see also Koutsouflakis, this volume; Koutzakiotis, this
volume). It should be noted that Gaidouronisi is an earlier name for Agathonisi, which continued to be used as
a pirate site in the following century (see Krantonelli 1998, 110, 179).

The archaeological research on Agathonisi
Agathonisi is located between Samos and the cluster of Dodecanese, connecting this area with the Ionian and
Carian coasts of Asia Minor. More generally, in the area west of Miletus and south of Samos there is a large
number of small islands and islets, of which, at least during the Hellenistic period, only Korsiai (Phournoi)
seems to have been Samian territory (Koutsouflakis, this volume). In particular, the islands of Lepsia (Leipsoi),
Arkitis (Arkioi), Patmos, Leros, Tragia (Agathonisi), Pharmakoussa (Pharmakonissi) and Lade (which in
­antiquity was an islet, although today it forms the Batmaz Tepeleri hill in the mainland region of Batiköy, see
 Greaves 2002, 3; Brückner et al. 2014, 86) belonged to the territory of Miletus, as evidenced by epigraphic and
 other evidence (Sarantidis 2020, 70−85; Fig. 2). Towers or/and fortifications of this period have been found on
 all these islands. Sarantidis (2020, 164, 192, 202−3) argues that these features performed a variety of functions:
 protection from pirates appears to have been the main one, but that they also played roles in trade, agricultural
 and craft production as well.

The vast majority of the bronze and silver coins found within the fortified settlement came from Miletus
(Triantafyllidis 2010, 22). Furthermore, the connection with Miletus is also revealed by a seal on a roof tile of
a public building, which states the following: “ἐπὶ τοῦ/τρίτου/θεοῦ πό/λεως ε/ὐλιμένου νίκης” (“during [the
period of] the third god of the well-harbored city victory”) (Fig. 8). From the study of the inscription, it follows
that when the god –who is identified by most scholars as Apollo Didymeus of Miletus– held the office of the
stephaniphoros for the third consecutive time, a victory of the “well-harbored city” occurred (Triantafyllidis
2015, 100−1; Sarantidis 2020, 80−1). The excavators conclude, therefore, that the roof tiles belonged to a public
building (a sanctuary?), dating to the third consecutive stephaniphoria of the Milesian Sanctuary of Apollo,
which will have occurred during the 2nd or the early 1st centuries BCE.
      During the same late 2nd−1st century BCE period, the excavators identified building modifications to
the interior spaces and the addition of new terracing at the site (Triantafyllidis 2015, 100; Sarantidis 2020,
160−62). According to the excavators, these additions possibly resulted from a construction program carried
out in ­coordination with a renewed Roman initiative along the coast of Asia Minor. During this period, the
Roman Senate passed the lex de provinciis praetoriis, calling on the cities of Asia Minor to actively cooperate in
the fight against the pirates, many of whom were employed as naval mercenaries by Mithridates (see de Souza
1999, 108−15; Geelhaar 2002). The rebuilding and reorganization of the defenses at Kastraki are attributed to
this Roman-inspired military mobilization (Triantafyllidis 2015, 98; Sarantidis 2020, 163−64). Eventually, the
main gate of the fortress on Agathonisi ceased to function and the entire settlement was filled and levelled by
a homogeneous layer before the middle of the 1st century BCE. Evidence of dated amphorae also ceases at this
time (Palamida et al. 2017, 85−90). Beside this gate, the purple-dye workshop was reorganized and expanded
to become the main activity of the settlement through the 1st century CE (Triantafyllidis 2010, 35; 2015, 100;
­Sarantidis 2020, 160−62). In other words, the excavation data from Kastraki reveal that the c­ haracter of the
 ­fortified settlement was not exclusively military. Significant evidence testifies to activities related to ­production
  and trade. It is certain that the military component to the settlement coexisted with its productive and
  ­commercial activities throughout the Hellenistic period (Triantafyllidis 2015, 101, 103; Sarantidis 2020, 163).

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Kastraki, Agathonisi: fortified installation for the sea defense of Miletus or pirate base?
The archaeological data from Kastraki raise questions about a possible connection to piracy. Based on the
­archaeological and epigraphic data presented briefly above, the excavator of the site, Dr. Pavlos ­Triantafyllidis,
 reasonably argues that the construction of this fortified installation was a state-sponsored project. It is un-
 deniable that both the period of use of this fort and its various building modifications and repairs in the late
 2nd−1st century BCE coincided with a period of intense pirate activity (Triantafyllidis 2015, 98; Sarantidis
 2020, 220−21). During this period, as Plutarch asserts (Pomp. 24.2–5), pirate fleets grew and multiplied, pirates
 took part as mercenaries in the conflicts of the hegemons, attacking merchant ships, islands, coastal cities and
 even large sanctuaries. Prominent men, who saw the potential for greater wealth and glory, likewise joined the
 pirates. Pirate ­harbors and roadsteads, fortresses and signal-stations were established throughout the seas, har-
 boring light and fast pirate ships, fully crewed with skillful sailors and warriors. On many shores, pirates tem-
 porarily took up residence, feasting and reveling while awaiting ransom for their captives. They often flaunted
 their success by decorating their warships with gilded sails and purple sails.
     Given this description by Plutarch, it is worth considering that the available evidence from Kastraki
­conforms perfectly with what is expected on a pirate base, based on the criteria listed above for a pirate base.
 First of all, the site at Kastraki was situated along a central sea route and with topographical features favorable
 to an anchorage. This put it proximate to maritime traffic. However, its topography rendered visible from sea
 only from limited vantage points. This offered the potential to assault victims by surprise. These features are
 familiar on sites chosen by pirates. The topography of the fortress calls to mind the words of Theophrastus
 (Char. 25.2), who describes as a coward the man who, when sailing at sea, thinks that every cape resembles a
 pirate ship. Moreover, the warlike character of this small settlement, results from its strong fortification and the
 rich and varied weaponry found at the site. The existence of a sanctuary and, above all, the abundance of finds
 that indicate trade and production activities make the settlement more likely to have been a permanent one
 as opposed to a temporary military garrison installed for the purpose of observing and pursuing potentially
 menacing warships.
    The maritime and trade orientation of its inhabitants, in combination with unique finds, such as the glass
skyphos, are not typical finds in a military environment, neither does Kastraki’s military identity accord with
the remains of an otherwise small settlement engaged in beekeeping and fishing activities. Coins, amphorae
and other objects from several regions (Triantafyllidis 2015, 100; Palamida et al. 2017, 90−93; Poupaki 2021,
131−3) do not necessarily imply direct trade relations with these cities, as the possibility that some of them
may have come from raids on passing ships from these regions cannot be ruled out (for the direct relationship
between trade and piracy, see Gabrielsen 2013, 147−53). Convinced that the site served as a fortress with an
anti-­piratical function, Sarantidis (2020, 164−65) attributes its relatively limited visibility to the inhabitants’
desire to guard their goods, pointing to the warehouses’ relative proximity to the military shipsheds. However,
this same proximity does not rule out the possibility that the warehouses served a need for unloading stolen
goods from raiding ships.
      Moreover, the two small shipsheds of Agathonisi are just as likely to have been used by pirates to maintain
their ships, the repeated cleaning of which was essential to maintain speed and maneuverability and as such
was systematically carried out by pirates until modern times (see also Koutzakiotis, this volume). Alongside
this function, the shipsheds may also have served to conceal the pirate ships and better enable their crews to
ambush potential victims (for pirate use of shipsheds, see Baika 2007–2008; Blackman et al. 2013, 238−41).
­Similar small naval stations (or roadsteads) with limited number of shipsheds have been found, among others,
 in ­Antikythera, ­Tripitos and Matala on Crete and in Ayios Dimitrios in the Krissaios Gulf (Blackman et al.
 2013, 231−53, 389−92, 518−24; Valavanis 2015; Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis, this volume; for pirate activity of
 Ηellenistic Crete see Brulé 1978; de Souza 1998; Perlman 1999). On the mentioned islet of Ayios Dimitrios, two
 shipsheds have been identified that serviced repairs and surprise raids on passing ships. This work is attributed
 by V­ alavanis (2015, 120) to the Aitolians, who occupied this area and were widely known for piratical activity
 (de Souza 1999, esp. 70-6; Grainger 1999, esp. 3–25; Scholten 2000).

The argument that the fortress of Agathonisi functioned as a pirate base is corroborated by the fact that it was
 founded and utilized during the Hellenistic period –when pirate activity was at its peak– as well as by the fact
 that, following the eradication of the pirates by the Romans, the function of the site transited to the ­production
of purple garments, for which Miletus was celebrated in Roman times (Sarantidis 2020, 199; on the production
of purple garments in Miletus, see Herrmann 1975). Moreover, the evidence of repairs and ­remodeling to the
fortress of Agathonisi, combined with the presence of weapons and stone and metal projectiles, indicate that
actual conflict occurred at the fortified settlement, which resulted from fending off of external attacks. A sim-
ilar scenario has been posited for the Antikythera fort (Tsaravopoulos 2004, 329, 335, 339–40; T      ­ saravopoulos
and Kroustalis, this volume), as well as for Vathy Limenari on Donoussa (Samaras 2015, 199), two sites that
have been suggested to have been used as pirate bases. Finally, it is also worth noting that the toponym Kleftos
(i.e., thieving) for the low mountain, at the foot of which the fort is situated, is a common name for places
where the pirates of the Ottoman and modern times concealed their treasure (Triantafyllidis 2006, 181; see also
­Krantonelli 1998, 110, 179). If one combines all this with the above-mentioned allusion of Strabo (14.1.7) to the
 presence of pirates lurking in hidden coves among the islands surrounding Miletus, the likelihood arises that
 the harbor of the fortified settlement of Agathonisi was one such cove.

The possible dual character of the fortress of Agathonisi
In view of all the issues raised above, is it possible that the fortress of Agathonisi was intended to protect the
­inhabitants of Miletus against pirates, and yet was on occasion exploited by pirates? As is known in the case of
 Antikythera (Tsaravopoulos 2004, 327–29; Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis, this volume), Aigilia was an outpost
 fortress of Phalasarna, that on occasion was employed by some of its inhabitants for purposes of p
                                                                                                  ­ iracy ­(Hadjidaki
 1988, 2020). The same situation appears to have occurred on the islet of Ayios Dimitrios in the Krissaios Gulf,
 which was intended to function as an outpost fortress of the Aitolian Chaleion, but very likely evolved into an
 Aitolian pirate base (Valavanis 2015, 120). The islet of Minoa in Megara seems to have ­functioned ­similarly:
although a fortress was established for the defense of the city, the inhabitants promptly used it to conduct pirate
raids (Thuc. 3.51.1). In the same manner that these sites were constructed in the aforementioned islands and
islets by powerful cities for defensive purposes, but they seem to have functioned for pirate activities as well, the
fortress at Agathonisi may have been used not only for the defense of the city of Miletus, but also for piracy. For
what it is worth, Ηellenistic towers have likewise been identified on the island of Lade, which is mentioned by
Strabo as a pirate base, as well as on the island of Pharmakoussa, where Julius Caesar’s pirates allegedly resided
(for these towers see Sarantidis 2020, 119–20 and 166–69, respectively).
    Of course, the cooperation of official authorities with pirates or even the practice of piracy by legitimate
naval fleets is hardly surprising. One such example is cited by Demosthenes (8.24−28) concerning the Athenian
general Diopeithes in the mid-4th century BCE. Lacking the necessary resources to conduct his naval opera-
tions, he actually resorted to offering “protection” for a fee to the Chians, the Erythraians and other Greek states
in Asia Minor, as well as engaging in overt acts of piracy by attacking merchant ships to feed and pay his troops
(de Souza 1999, 36−8). Another incident of cooperation between a well-known city and pirates is described by
Polyaenus (Strat. 5.19.1): Aenetus, who is described as a general of Demetrius I Poliorcetes and the commander
of Ephesus’ garrison, regularly offered shelter to pirates willing to maraud neighboring areas. However, Poly-
aenus continues, Lysimachus’ general Lycos was able to bribe one such pirate chief named Andron, who was
using Ephesus as his base, to betray its defenses and thereby enable Lysimachus to seize the settlement. In other
words, pirates were very often employed by legitimate authorities, provided, of course, such a situation was
mutually beneficial.
    In short, a similar argument can be made for the fortress of Kastraki on Agathonisi. This settlement could
certainly have functioned as an outpost fortress of Miletus and cooperated with the city, as the numerous finds
that connect it with the city reveal. At the same time, however, the people who lived there −or, at least, some of
them− alongside their other activities, may very likely have engaged in systematic, seasonal or opportunistic

­parties or as adversaries. The coexistence of military, artisanal and commercial activities, as evidenced by the

findings.evidence_excerpt:
In summary, this paper does not dispute the likelihood that the fortified settlement on the islet of Agathonisi
was an outpost fortress employed by the city of Miletus to defend against threats by sea, just as the other islets
of the same city probably functioned. What is argued here is that the fortress could have possessed another
dimension, that of its use by pirates, either systematically or occasionally. This alternate dimension is indicated
by many of the archaeological remains that have come to light from the systematic excavation and study of
the site and is supported by the ancient sources, particularly by Strabo’s reference to pirate activity on “the
isles in the neighborhood of the Tragaeae” (14.1.7, trans. H.L. Jones, Cambridge, Mass., 1929). Thus, since the
­archaeological data from the excavation of the fort at Katraki on Agathonisi fit most of the criteria mentioned
 at the beginning of this study and in what is expected of a pirate base, and since the sources implicitly indicate
 this, it needs to be considered as such.
    The simultaneous use of the islets for pirate and non-pirate activities does not necessarily pose a problem
to this interpretation. On the contrary, this seems to have been the predominant nature of piracy, since, as the
sources confirm, pirates never engaged solely in this occupation, but rather they were active members of society
and carried out various activities, including piracy. It, therefore, needs to be recognized that the main step in
finding the archaeological evidence of piracy requires that we come to terms with the frequency of piracy in
antiquity as well as its character. Likewise, the methodology of the archaeology of piracy is important for the
identification of the archaeological data associated with this behavior. Thus, not only from the sources, but also
from the archaeological data, it is possible to comprehend how deserted and remote islets became crucial sites
for pirates diachronically, as they could serve many of their activities. The topographical data of the islets reveal
ideal features for pirate bases, for lookout posts, for hiding places, for lurking and ambush, for temporary setups
for the distribution of booty or the short term stays for ransom payments, for the concealment of booty, for the
concealment of evidence of piratical activity, and generally for temporary places to evade the gaze of eyes of the
rest of the world. Thus, isolated islets, which very often remain isolated from archaeological research as well,
constitute a fertile ground for the identification of archaeological data of piracy.
    On the assumption that piracy can eventually be identified archaeologically, we hope for the wider use of the
methodology of the archaeology of piracy by scholars and for the eventual identification not only of pirate bases
in the countless islets of Greek seas, but also of other manifestations of the archaeological evidence of piracy.
The new methodology should not only be applied to ongoing and future archaeological investigations, but also
to the data that already exists from past excavations. And that is because, “the real voyage of discovery consists
not in seeking new landscapes, but in having new eyes” (Proust 1927, 559).

The Case of Hellenistic Rhodes

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Throughout classical antiquity, several naval powers attempted to eliminate piracy, as this activity represented a constant
threat to human safety and the efficient conduct of maritime trade. Among these powers, Hellenistic Rhodes holds an
exceptional place, due to its systematic efforts for the elimination of pirate activity, which was at its peak during this
period. This paper examines the relationship between Rhodes and the pirates, and in particular the causes behind the
Rhodian anti-piracy policy and the ways in which this policy was pursued. The design of the trihemiolia –a type of light
and extremely fast ship, capable of pursuing the pirate hemioliai that stormed the Hellenistic Aegean– undoubtedly had
a crucial part to play in the Rhodians’ anti-piracy actions, the highlight of which was the victory of Rhodes in the First
Cretan War at the end of the 3rd century BCE. The analysis of the relevant historical and archaeological data attempted
in this paper reveals that piracy was a decisive factor in both the establishment of Rhodes as a leading naval power in the
Hellenistic Aegean and its decline.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Throughout classical antiquity, Rhodes was an important trading center of the Aegean and the eastern
­Mediterranean, but it rose to prominence during the Hellenistic period. As discussed in detail below, the Rho-
 dians are praised by ancient authors as “masters of the sea”, mainly due to their systematic efforts to ­eliminate
 piracy. This paper examines the relationship between the Rhodians and pirates, as Hellenistic Rhodes is an
 excellent case study of how the naval powers were dealing with the phenomenon of piracy. It opens with a brief
 discussion of the relationship between trade and piracy, as it was this relationship that determined the attitude
 of each naval power towards pirates. Subsequently, the various aspects of Rhodes’ anti-piracy policy and the
 ways in which it sought to enforce this policy are examined. Finally, the conflict between the Rhodians and the
 Cretan pirates is examined, which had a decisive impact on both the prosperity and the decline of Hellenistic
 Rhodes.

important factors damaging trade and, consequently, the economy of cities (e.g., Ormerod 1924, 113, 128, 155.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
ore recent scholars, arguing that the economic growth of trade in the Mediterranean area during the
1st and 2nd centuries CE was thanks to suppression of piracy by the Romans (e.g., Hopkins 1983, xviii–xix).
­Besides, the contrasting relationship between trade and piracy seems to be confirmed by ancient authors, such
 as ­Thucydides (1.5.1, 1.13.5) and Strabo (e.g., 3.2.5, 10.4.9).
    Recent research has offered a different perspective on this previously held belief. Shipwrecks, as well as
amphorae distributed in large ­quantities and in various places, prove that trade in the Aegean continued un-
interrupted, even during periods of intense pirate activity (Parker 1992, 31–5; Davies 2001, 27–9; Gabrielsen
2013a, 149, with further bibliography). Interestingly, during the second half of the 3rd century BCE –a period of
economic prosperity in the C­ yclades and the flourishing of important commercial ports, such as Thasos, Delos,
Kos and Rhodes itself– there was a significant increase in pirate attacks (Gabrielsen 2001, 221).
    Contrary to what was generally accepted in the past, scholars now perceive trade and piracy as two closely
related forms of economic activity (e.g., Gabrielsen 2001, 221; Samaras 2015, 191). Goods and people stolen
by pirates gradually began to reach the markets of the Aegean and neighboring regions (Rauh 1997; 1999, 171;
de Souza 1999, 22, 56, 201–2). Pirates seem to have been the main supplier of slaves, as they served various
trading centers, the most famous being Delos (cf. Strabo 14.5.2). Some scholars have claimed that the pirates’
main aim was the enslavement of people (e.g., Marόti 1969–1970, 70; Brulé 1978, 18, 159, 161, 183), while de
Souza (1999, 60–3) later considered statements about the piratical contribution to the Hellenistic slave trade to
be highly exaggerated. However, the fact that Hellenistic cities protected their citizens from being snatched and
enslaved suggests the gravity and frequency of the risk (Lewis 2019, 93–9). Regardless of the actual size of the
pirates’ contribution to the slave trade, it is plausible that it was vital for them to find markets to sell their prey,
and more than a few cities were willing to provide them with port bases and markets for their ill-gotten goods
(de Souza 1999, 188).
    It can therefore be concluded that trade and piracy have more in common than might have been expected.
These are activities with a similar motive (i.e., the economic gain of the participants), which fulfill their purpose
only when their products reach the markets to be sold. On the other hand, it should not be forgotten that trade
was a non-violent practice and that merchants were in direct danger from pirates, as they risked being enslaved
or even dying and losing their goods if they were confronted with a pirate ship. Pirates, for their part, sought to
keep maritime trade going uninterrupted and even chose to operate in new places from time to time so as not
to exhaust the merchants of a single region (de Souza 1995, 187–88). Finally, for the markets it was immaterial
whether the cargo came from stolen goods or not (Gabrielsen 2013a, 148–49).
    As far as Rostovzeef ’s statement (Rostovzeef 1941, 1242–243) that the economic development of cities was
harmed by piracy is concerned, it is obviously only partially true. Τhe cities targeted and plundered by the pi-
rates were indeed damaged, both economically and materially. But other cities, those that provided a market for
piratical goods, prospered as a result. The cities that cooperated with the pirates for their economic growth were
not few. In fact, piracy was a solution for the poor habitants of a region, since it was probably a conscious choice
that was linked to socio-economic and political dimensions (Davies 1984, 290; Gabrielsen 2001, 221–22).
    Several ancient authors confirm that it was common practice for the Hellenistic cities to recruit pirates as
mercenaries, when there was a need for sea or infantry forces (e.g., Dem. 23.148–149, 162, 166–167; Strabo
10.4.10). During this period, the distinction between pirates and mercenaries is often quite blurred, as the same
people could engage in both activities (Ormerod 1924, 143). The fact that the cities recruited pirates as merce-
naries suggests acceptance of the practice of piracy, but the trust they placed in these people often turned out
to be misplaced, since pirates did not hesitate to betray their commanders if a better economic deal was offered
(Pacheco 2020, 102).

Demetrius I Poliorcetes, who cooperated with the pirate Timocles in the unsuccessful siege of Rhodes in 305–
304 BCE (Diod. Sic. 20.97.5). He also recruited to his army merchant ship captains, who followed them appar-

fluid context between pirates, merchants and mercenaries. Merchants could turn into mercenaries just as easily
as pirates if a profitable opportunity arose (Gabbert 1986, esp. 156; Pacheco 2020, 102).
    For the Rhodian side, on the other hand, there are no reports of the use of pirates as mercenaries in their
military conflicts, nor of the granting of markets or harbor bases to pirates. Even during the troubled ­Hellenistic
times, pirates and their prey were not welcome in all commercial ports, as Rostovtzeff had argued (1941, 196; for
arguments against Rostovtzeff ’s view, see Lewis 2019, 100–1). However, as discussed in more detailed below, this
did not prevent Rhodians from overlooking piracy, when it worked in their interests. It is therefore e­ xtremely
interesting to study the perspective of a city economically dependent on maritime trade and how it dealt with
the long-standing problem of piracy to preserve its economic vitality.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
During the Hellenistic period, Rhodes based its economic prosperity on maritime trade, especially long-­
distance trade. The island’s most important trading partner was Egypt, “for it happened that most of their
revenues were due to the merchants who sailed to Egypt, and that in general the city drew its food supply
from that kingdom” (Diod. Sic. 20.81.4, trans. R.M. Geer, Cambridge, Mass., 1954). The city was provided
with five harbors, which were naturally fortified thanks to the topography of the island (Gabrielsen 1997, 37–9;
­Filimonos-Tsopotou 2004, 46–70, with further bibliography). The Rhodians, however, did not content with this,
 but proceeded to build fortifications and walls to strengthen the protection of the bog and the harbors (for the
 impressive ­fortification system of Hellenistic Rhodes see Filimonos-Tsopotou 2004; Manoussou-Ntella 2016).
    According to several ancient authors, the Rhodians constantly tried to suppress piracy during the Hellenistic
period. Among the naval power of classical antiquity, few seem to have made such intense and systematic efforts
to control this phenomenon as Rhodes. Strabo praises the Rhodians for the care “with which they administered
affairs of state generally, and particularly those relative to their marine” and thanks to which they became “for
a long period masters of the sea” and “they put an end to piracy” (Strabo 14.2.5, trans. W. Falconer, London,
1903). Similarly, Diodorus refers that “the city of the Rhodians […] was strong in sea power” and that “she
advanced to such strength that in behalf of the Greeks she by herself undertook her war against the pirates and
purged the seas of these evil-doers” (Diod. Sic. 20.82.1, trans. R.M. Geer, Cambridge, Mass., 1954). Even in
the 2nd century CE, Aelius Aristides mentions with admiration the enormous booty the Rhodians had seized
from the Tyrrhenian pirates and points out that they once “ruled the seas” (Aristid. Or. 24.53, trans. C.A. Behr,
Leiden, 1981). In addition, thanks to Rhodes, merchant ships were often escorted by warships or with armed
men on board, to ensure the safety of the crew and the cargo during the voyage (e.g., Diod. Sic. 20.82.2; Lycurg.
Leoc. 18). But how far are these statements true? Can the Rhodians really be described as “masters of the sea”
in the Hellenistic period?
    There is little but significant evidence for Rhodian anti-piracy actions. In 220 BCE they drove off Demetrius
of Pharos from the Cyclades, which he was plundering (Polyb. 4.19.8; see also Davies 2004). Also, in 200 BCE
they acted against pirates from Chalkis raiding Attica, and in 190 BCE they protected the strait of Kephalonia
from pirates, in both cases with the help of the Romans and their allies (Livy 31.22.5–7, 37.13.11–12; see also
de Souza 1999, 86, 88; Gabrielsen 2001, 228, 230). The Rhodians even played an important role in the great
campaign against piracy with the measures of the “Lex de provinciis praetoriis”. This law appears to date from
around 100 BCE and survives in two versions, one found at Delphi and one from Knidos (Crawford 1996,
231–70; de Souza 1999, 108–14). Additionally, the involvement of the Rhodian navy in anti-piracy actions is
further ­confirmed by certain inscriptions, which are discussed in more detail below.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Gabrielsen rightly argues that these are just a few examples of the great effort of the Rhodians to protect the
seas from pirates, as the inscriptions record actions against piracy as a common phenomenon. Furthermore,
in the peace treaty between Rhodes and the Cretan city of Hierapytna about the end of the 3rd century BCE,
the former show a keen interest in pirates and those accepting them in their ports (see in more detail below,
“Rhodes and the Cretan pirates”). Finally, by the last quarter of the 3rd century BCE Rhodes could boast of
both the resilience of its maritime infrastructure and the good use of it (Gabrielsen 2001, 229). It is indicative
that in that period Rhodes had managed to control many offshore naval bases from present-day Kastellorizo to
Antikythera (ancient Aigilia) and from eastern Crete to as far away as Delos (Gabrielsen 1997, 41–2).
   The Rhodian navy included ships distinguished for their speed and agility, the phylakidai nees (φυλακίδαι
νῆες), which means guardships in ancient Greek (Diod. Sic. 20.93.2; see also Gabrielsen 1997, 108–9; 2013b, 74).
The name of these ships clearly refers to their use, as they were designed in such a way as to provide protection
against raiders. Rhodian phylakidai were mainly intended for special missions, perhaps against pirate attacks,
even giving them this name in order to advertise their effectiveness (Gabrielsen 2001, 230).
    The use of phylakidai is revealed by a series of inscriptions referring to this type of ship. By way of example,
the inscription IG XI.4 596 from Delos, dating after 250 BCE, mentions that a Rhodian navarch and his three
trierarchs received honors for ensuring “the protection [φυλακῆς] of the islands and the safety [σωτηρίαι] of
the Greeks”, presumably against pirates (Holleaux 1907, 359 n. 4; de Souza 1999, 81; Gabrielsen 2001, 230;
Constantakopoulou 2017, 150–51). In another Delian inscription, of the early 2nd century BCE, the Rhodian
navarch Epikrates is honored for “the safety [ἀσφαλείας] of the shipping trade and the protection [φυλακῆς]
of the islands”, as well as for the fact that he took care to issue a regulation that no one of his crews should use
Delos as a naval base (ὁρμηθῶσιν) in their piratical raids (πειρατεύοντες) against enemy (IG XI.4 751; de Souza
1999, 87–8; Gabrielsen 2001, 230–31; Constantakopoulou 2017, 151). The same navarch also participated in the
chase of pirates off Kephalonia in 190 BCE, which has already been mentioned (Livy 37.13.11–12). In general,
the Delian inscription corpus includes several cases attesting to the protection provided to the island by the
Rhodians (e.g., IG XI.4 1133 [ca. 300–250 BCE], 1135 [mid-3rd century BCE] and 752–753 [beginning of the
2nd century BCE]).
   However, beyond the protection they offered, the Rhodians also acted as a means of securing trade relations
and administering justice among merchants. In 220 BCE, Rhodes declared war against Byzantion, because the
Aegean merchants had turned to them for help, as Polybius recounts:

findings.evidence_excerpt:
It is therefore clear that, during the Hellenistic period, Rhodes was a dominant naval force. With their navy
 the Rhodians chased pirates, protected the islands and merchant ships, while Aegean trading communities
 facing serious problems turned to them for help. However, to complete the picture of the Rhodians as “­ masters
of the sea”, three further comments need to be made: firstly, for Rhodian protection and help, the island’s allies
often paid exorbitant sums in return, significantly boosting the economy and, by extension, the naval power of
Rhodes (Gabrielsen 2001, 233–35). Secondly, the effort to suppress pirate activity was not generalized and un-
conditional, but depended on the political and economic interests of Rhodes (Pacheco 2020, 101). For ­example,
as Strabo comments (14.5.2), the Rhodians did not intervene when Cilician pirates were harassing the ­Seleucids
in the eastern Mediterranean, as they were themselves hostile to this dynasty. Thirdly, when necessary, the
­Rhodians themselves carried out attacks and raids against merchant ships, producing maritime violence for
 their own benefit (e.g., Diod. Sic. 20.93.2–5).

It is obvious that the navy of Rhodes played a key role in the island’s effort to eliminate piracy. Even if the claim
that the Rhodian navy “was particularly designed as an antipirate force” (Berthold 1984, 98) seems exaggerated,
there is some direct evidence for its action against the pirates. Diodorus mentions a Rhodian law according to
which “the bodies of those who fell in the war should be given public burial”, while there was also a provision
for support for the families of the dead at public cost (Diod. Sic. 20.84.3, trans. R.M. Geer, Cambridge, Mass.,
1954). This custom is attested by a funerary inscription found on the island that honors three brothers who lost
their lives fighting for the Rhodian navy:

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The most probably date for this inscription is about the middle of the 3rd century BCE (Sekunda 2014;
see also Gabrielsen 2001, 229, n. 43). For the third brother, Polemarchos, it is clearly mentioned that he died
fighting against the pirates (τοὺς λαϊστὰς), but most scholars accept that the other two brothers were killed in a
similar way (e.g., Ormerod 1924, 130 n. 3; de Souza 1999, 50–1). The Tyrrhenians mentioned in relation to the
two brothers may represent any pirates of the Adriatic Sea or the Italian peninsula (on the Tyrrhenian pirates
see Bakhuizen 1988; Bresson 2007; Fritzilas, this volume). Polemarchos is also mentioned in another inscription
from the island, which is earlier, dating back to the beginning of the 3rd century BCE (Jacopi 1932, 169–70). In
this second inscription, he is honored for his participation in an attack on Aigilia (present-day Antikythera),
once more against pirates (Brulé 1978, 31; de Souza 1999, 51; Bresson 2016, 162–63; see also Tsaravopoulos and
Kroustalis, this volume).
   Another inscription offering valuable information about the actions of the Rhodian navy against the pirates
comes from an impressive monument discovered on the acropolis of Lindos: a marble prow of a warship, on
which a statue (probably Nike) once stood (Blinkenberg 1938, 30–7; 1941, 301–13 no. 88; Filimonos-Tsopotou
2013, 269–70; Gabrielsen 2013c, 69–71; Figs. 1–2). The preserved part of the inscription of this monument,
which was dated between 265 and 260 BCE based on the letter forms and prosopographical data ­(Blinkenberg
1941, 308; see also Gabrielsen 2013c, 70 n. 24), testifies that it was dedicated to Lindos’ principal deity, Athena
Lindia, by the commanders and crews of a squadron of trihemioliai as a tithe (ἀπαρχὰν) from the booty
(λαφύρων) they had captured during a successful naval expedition. Blinkenberg argued that this expedition was
against Tyrrhenian pirates, a view accepted by most scholars (e.g., Filimonos-Tsopotou 2013, 269; Gabrielsen
2013c, 71–2; contra Wiemer 2002, 134).
    This inscribed monument raises many interesting issues for discussion, but the present paper is limited to
commenting on two specific aspects. Firstly, in this case the booty resulting from the successful expedition
against the Tyrrhenians did not become state property, but was claimed by the crews, which reveals that at
least in Hellenistic Rhodes private anti-pirate campaigns could be organized and conducted (Gabrielsen 2013c,
71–2). Secondly, considering the cost of this impressive monument and the fact that it was dedicated as a tithe
of the booty, it becomes clear that these campaigns could yield a very substantial profit (Wiemer 2002, 134),
which explains the private interest in them. Moreover, of particular importance is that the expedition against
the Tyrrhenians was carried out with trihemioliai, a ship type developed by the Rhodians specifically for their
anti-pirate operations.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Furthermore, in the battle of Chios in 201 BCE, the existence of trihemioliai (τριημιολίαι) in the allied fleets
of Attalus and Rhodes, which defeated the fleet of Philip V of Macedonia, is mentioned by Polybius (16.2.10).
Apart from the references of the ancient writers, there is a series of inscriptions attesting to the Rhodian origin
of the trihemiolia (for an overview of this inscription corpus see Blinkenberg 1938, 14–19).
    But why did the Rhodians design the trihemiolia and incorporate it in their fleet? During the 4th century
BCE, pirate hemioliai were very successful, as they were light and extremely fast, making the traditional ships
of the Greek fleets up to that time unsuitable for their pursuit (for hemioliai see Casson 1958, 14–16; Morrison
1980, 121–24; Nakas, this volume, with further bibliography). It is illustrative that Theophrastus, who lived at
that time, mentions ships as a synonym for the pirate threat (Theophr. Char. 25.2). The Rhodians sought a solu-
tion to the difficulty of pursuing pirate hemioliai by adapting to the traditional model of the trireme elements of
the hemiolia (Casson 1958, 17). The result was the trihemiolia, a ship type heavier and faster than the hemiolia,
suitable for both pursuit and combat.
    The trihemiolia was used exclusively as part of the organized navy and not as a pirate ship (Casson 1958,
16, n. 16). Its ­effectiveness in the pursuit of pirate ships contributed significantly to the establishment of the
reputation of the Rhodians as “masters of the sea”. So strong is the connection between the Rhodian navy and
the ­trihemioliai, that the ships both in the aforementioned monument of 265–250 BCE, dedicated to Athena
Lindia, and in other well-known monuments (e.g., the relief prow below the entrance to the acropolis of Lindos
and the ­famous Nike of Samothrace; Figs. 3–4) were long considered to be trihemioliai (e.g., Blinkenberg 1938,
22–40; ­Morrison 1980, 124–25; Rice 1996, 214; Mark 1998, 157–58), a view now seriously disputed (Casson
1971, 102–3; ­Gabrielsen 1997, 88–9; Stewart 2016, 404, 407–8; Clinton et al. 2020, 565–67; Palagia 2021, 155).

findings.evidence_excerpt:
As already mentioned, during the Hellenistic period Rhodes made systematic efforts to eliminate piracy. These
efforts lasted until about the end of the Second Cretan War (153 BCE), which found Rhodes extremely ­weakened
and Rome gaining the role that Rhodes had occupied until then. The primary objective of the Rhodians was to
patrol the seas and ensure the safety of trade, as this served their economic interests (Brulé 1978, 29–30). In the
Rhodians’ anti-piracy operations, the main targets seem to have been the Cretans, who had developed intense
pirate activity, especially towards the end of the 3rd century BCE, when Philip V of Macedonia encouraged this
activity in order to harm Rhodes economically and militarily, aiming to make his kingdom the leading Aegean
power (for the Cretan piracy see Brulé 1978; de Souza 1999, esp. 80–4; Perlman 1999).
